messages.subject: Re: plots unaffected by alpha (mac)
messages.body_plain:
Hum... on my PC everything works fine, but on my mac both of the
following produce identical (non-transparent) results:

> qplot(carat, price, data = diamonds)

> qplot(carat, price, data = diamonds, alpha = I(1/50))

Your explicitly layered call does produce the correct result though:

> ggplot(aes(x = carat, y = price), data = diamonds) +
+    geom_point(colour = alpha('black', 1/50))

so does

qplot(carat, price, data = diamonds, colour = I(alpha("black",1/50)))

I just installed the package last night, so it should be the latest
version. I'll see if upgrading to 2.9.0 helps, but looking at the
documentation, I don't see why 'alpha=I(1/50)' should even work. The
docs imply that it should be going into the ... argument, which is
then passed to geom_point. geom_point doesn't have an alpha argument,
so again it goes into the ... but this is "unused" according to it's
documentation, so how is my system's behavior not expected?

messages.subject: Mean lines with stat_summary() not showing up
messages.subject_clean: Mean lines with stat_summary() not showing up
messages.body_plain:
I'm doing a scatterplot with a categorical variable on the x axis, and another categorical variable that's color-coded. I also want to add in lines that track the mean values, but they're not showing up.

I'll illustrate what I'm trying to do, using the diamonds data (I hope the inline images show up properly):

dsmall <- diamonds[sample(nrow(diamonds), 100), ]

# No lines show up
qplot(color, carat, data=dsmall, colour=cut,

      position=position_jitter(width=.25, height=0)) +
    stat_summary(fun.y=mean, geom="line")

# It works if you convert the x-axis variable from a factor to numeric

qplot(as.numeric(color), carat, data=dsmall, colour=cut,
      position=position_jitter(width=.25, height=0)) +
    stat_summary(fun.y=mean, geom="line")

# It works if you use bars for the mean values
qplot(color, carat, data=dsmall, colour=cut,
      position=position_jitter(width=.25, height=0)) +
    stat_summary(fun.y=mean, geom="bar", position=position_dodge())

So it looks like the problem has something to do with trying to use lines with categorical variables. Is this the expected behavior, and if so, how does one work around it?

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: Mean lines with stat_summary() not showing up
messages.subject_clean: Mean lines with stat_summary() not showing up
messages.body_plain:
Hi Winston,

You need

qplot(color, carat, data=dsmall, colour=cut,
      position=position_jitter(width=.25, height=0)) +

    stat_summary(aes(group = cut), fun.y=mean, geom="line")

See section 4.5.3 of the book for why.

Hadley

messages.subject: geom_abline - gradient does not work?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Hadley et al.,

This works as expected:

mydata <- data.frame(x = 1:10, y = 1:10)
qplot(x, y, data = mydata) + geom_abline(intercept = 0, gradient = 1)

So does this:

qplot(x, y, data = mydata) + geom_abline(intercept = 5, gradient = 1)

But this does not:

qplot(x, y, data = mydata) + geom_abline(intercept = 0, gradient = 2)

...seems that it is not picking up on the value of intercept.

David

messages.subject: stat_sum and uneval data trouble
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I am new in using R and ggplot2 so forgive me if my question sounds
too ..primitive..

I have some survey data on a csv file and I calculate from certain
pairs of questions some variables in the following way (its an
example):

hyp1x <- (d$q7!='1')+(d$q8!='1')
#Calculate x for the first hypothesis

hyp1y <- (d$q15=='No')+(d$q16=='No')+(d$q17=='No')
#Calculate y for the first hypothesis

so according to a table entry (answer) I give or not a score on the
hypothesis X axis and hypothesis Y.

Then I want to map those on a summary of values according to the
"score". I did use:

plot(hyp1x,hyp1y)

which gave an ugly result, similar results would not show
"scored" (summed) but only as circles on top of circles..

I was adviced to use stat_sum (http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/stat_sum.html)
and it looks the most suitable for what I want to do, a simple sum on
the dimentions of x,y. However, with the following code:

tmp <- ggplot(aes(x = hyp1x, y = hyp1y))
tmp + stat_sum(aes(group = 1))

 I get this error:

Error: ggplot2 doesn't know how to deal with data of class uneval

How could I check the data class?... it is a simple sum of the
answered questions and I thought it wouldnt be such a problem. Any tip
or advice would be most welcome!

Theodoros , a R/ggplot2er in early steps

messages.body_plain:
Dear Hadley et al. -- I am a relative newbie to R in the learning
phase of ggplot2 and, while amazed by its power and potential, am
having some difficulty coming up with the appropriate code for my
desired plot (trying to help out a colleague).   Was hoping I could
get some input from the masters!

My (colleague's) data setup: rats nested within treatment groups,
responses then measured over time for each rat.  Easy enough for me to
get the data in long format appropriate for, say, lme(), which I am
assuming is desirable for ggplot2 as well.  Code below creates a
simplified version of the data I'm working with, though with random
values for the response that won't differ on average by group (while
the real data presumably will):

resp <- sample(100, replace=TRUE)
group <- rep(1:2, each=50)
rat <- rep(1:10, each=10)
time <- rep(1:10, length=100)
mydata <- data.frame(rat, group, time, resp)

1) main plot:  I am interested in plotting time (x) against resp (y),
with one line per group, adding vertical error bars, lines and error
bars representing the mean and standard error for rats within that
group.

2) bonus feature:  the first three time points per rat are a baseline,
so separating the line connecting those three with the line connecting
the rest of the time points would be wonderful.  Obviously, I can code
baseline vs. experiment as a separate factor in the data if need be.

My desired plot seems quite similar to, say, Figure 5.15 (right panel)
from the ggplot2 book, but I am having difficulty translating the code
for that plot to suit my purposes.  I imagine I need to use the
summary functions that access the Hmisc functions for standard errors,
but again, just am not yet "up to speed" enough to manage it on my
own.  Taking into account the nesting (so that lines connects means of
groups rather than each rat) is tricky for me for some reason, though
I know it shouldn't be!

Many thanks in advance for any help/advice you can provide.

-Keith

messages.subject: Re: error bars for nested data + separation of line segments (newbie)
messages.subject_clean: error bars for nested data + separation of line segments (newbie)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Keith,

Here's how I'd go about it - the key to both aspects of your problem
is setting up grouping correctly.

Hadley

resp <- sample(100, replace=TRUE)
group <- rep(1:2, each=50)
rat <- rep(1:10, each=10)
time <- rep(1:10, length=100)

rats <- data.frame(rat, group, time, resp)

library(ggplot2)
# Starting point
qplot(time, resp, data = rats)
# Split up by groups
qplot(time, resp, data = rats) +
  facet_grid(~ group)
# Draw line for each rat
qplot(time, resp, data = rats, geom = "line", group = rat) +
  facet_grid(~ group)
# Uhoh, bug in ggplot2 :(  Work around:
rats$g <- rats$group
qplot(time, resp, data = rats, geom = "line", group = rat) +
  facet_grid(~ g)

# Add mean lines and error bars
qplot(time, resp, data = rats, geom = "line", group = rat) +
  facet_grid(~ g) +
  stat_summary(aes(group = 1), fun.y = mean,
    geom = "line", colour = "red") +
  stat_summary(aes(group = time), fun.data = mean_cl_normal,
    geom = "pointrange", colour = "red")
# The important thing to note in the above plot is the grouping:
#  we want one line for each panel, so group = 1
#  and error bars for each time, so time = 1

# To separate baseline points from treated, you use grouping
# in a similar way:
qplot(time, resp, data = rats, geom = "line",
  group = interaction(rat, time <= 3)) + facet_grid(~ g)

messages.subject: Draw additional stuff with grid
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I want to draw a circle on top of a ggplot. The circle is of known
diameter measured in the same dimensions as the axes (everything is in
cm).

I don't want to "cheat" with solution such as drawing a open circle
symbol of very large size, or approximating the circle with a
geom_path. So I figure the way to do it is to dive into grid and
modify stuff in the guts of the plot. However I have a problem of
scales:

# produce the base plot
qplot(0,0) + xlim(-5,5) + ylim(-5,5)

# examine the viewport stack
grid.ls <http://grid.ls>(viewport=T)
current.vpTree()
# at that point, I can see that the data point is in panel-3-3
# Q.1: is there any easy/foolproof way to get that programatically?

# naviguate to this view port
current.viewport()
seekViewport("panel-3-3")
current.viewport()
current.vpPath()

# draw stuff
grid.circle(0,0,0.5)
# but these coordinates are relative to the bottom left of the window,
while I want the circule to be drawn relative to the scales of the
current plot. According to chapter 5 of the grid book (p.160), I sould
do:
grid.circle(0,0,0.5, default.units="native")
# but this does not work
# Q. 2: what am I missing here?

# and actually, even though I navigated to "panel-3-3", the
GRID.circle grobs seem to be in a separate tree
grid.ls <http://grid.ls>(viewport=T)

upViewport(0)
current.viewport()
grid.ls <http://grid.ls>(viewport=T)

Thanks in advance for your help.

JiHO

messages.subject: Incompatibility with package circular
messages.body_plain:
Hi again

(it seems it's bug uncovering day for me today ;) )

ggplot choques on objects produced by the package "circular", which is
meant to deal with angles. circular introduces as new "circular" class
which gives useful information such as rotation direction, unit,
origin etc. Objects of class circular are also of class numeric so
ggplot should be able to deal with that part.

library("ggplot2")
install.packages("circular")
library("circular")

t=data.frame(theta=runif(10), y=runif(10))
qplot(theta, y, data=t)
t=data.frame(y=runif(10), theta=runif(10))
# works ok

t$theta=circular(t$theta)

class(t$theta)
[1] "circular" "numeric"

qplot(theta, y, data=t)
Error in if (test == TRUE) { : argument is of length zero

ggplot(t)+geom_point(aes(x=theta, y=y))
Error in if (test == TRUE) { : argument is of length zero

ggplot(t)+geom_path(aes(x=theta, y=y))
Error in if (test == TRUE) { : argument is of length zero

ggplot(t)+geom_bar(aes(x=theta))
Error in if (test == TRUE) { : argument is of length zero

On this one I am stumped. I can't even find a "if (test == TRUE)" bit
in ggplot's code...

PS: for now:

t$theta = as.numeric(t$theta)
class(t$theta)
[1] "numeric"
ggplot(t)+geom_bar(aes(x=theta))

solves the problem.

JiHO

messages.subject: Re: qqline in ggplot2?
messages.body_plain:
Compute the slope & intercept beforehand:

slope = (quantile(data$residual,p=.75)-quantile(data$residual,.25))/(qnorm(.75)-qnorm(.25))
intercept = quantile(data$residual,.25) - slope*qnorm(.25)
qq_line = data.frame(intercept=intercept,slope=slope)

Then:

ggplot(data, na.rm=T) +
geom_point(aes(sample=residual), stat="qq",distribution=qnorm) +
geom_abline(
     data = qq_line
     ,aes(
          intercept = intercept
          ,slope=slope
     )
)

messages.subject: [SOLVED] Re: Arrow heads inexplicably missing
messages.body_plain:
On 2009-May-02  , at 22:31 , JiHO wrote:

> Has someone remarked this already:

No one probably has because this is just me being dumb. I did not
realize that the arrow argument only added an arrow to the *last* bit
of the path, and not to every step.

system("wget http://dl.getdropbox.com/u/1047321/x.csv")
x = read.csv("x.csv")

# the arrow head is actually there but not very visible
ggplot(x) + geom_path(aes(x=x,y=y), arrow=arrow())
ggplot(x) + geom_path(aes(x=x,y=y), arrow=arrow(length=unit(3,"inch")))

# with separation in bits by color for example, I get an arrow head
per step
ggplot(x) + geom_path(aes(x=x,y=y, colour=X), arrow=arrow())
# where X (capital) is the row number

# I don't particularly care about the colour so the key here is to use
grouping so split the path in its sub units. But of course, splitting
it in units of one point does not work:
ggplot(x) + geom_path(aes(x=x,y=y, group=X), arrow=arrow())
# so I just need to trick ggplot and have two successive points in
each group
y = x[-1,]
y$X = y$X-1
x = rbind(x,y)
ggplot(x) + geom_path(aes(x=x,y=y, group=X), arrow=arrow())
# yay!

Sorry to have bothered you all with that.

JiHO

messages.body_plain:

When making a graph with both lines and points, is there a way to have the lines not be drawn inside the points, or stop short of touching the points? 3, 2, 1.5, 1)), .Names = c("subject", "xval", "yval"), row.names = c(NA,
10L), class = "data.frame")

qplot(xval, yval, data=df, geom=c("point"), shape=subject, size=I(3)) +

    scale_shape_manual(value = c(1,19)) +

ggplot(df, aes(xval, yval, shape = subject)) +
  geom_line(size = 2) +

messages.subject: Re: Combination of stacking and dodging

Currently, there's no way to combine stacking and dodging in a single
layer (and I'm not sure even how it could work, in terms of separating

faceting, because you'll be able to put the labels on the bottom of
the plot, and format them so they look like regular labels.  Hopefully
that will be easy after I've rewritten the layout code this summer.

messages.subject: Re: Standard deviation and stacked barcharts
messages.body_plain:
> I would have expected "width" to be a parameter and not an aesthetic in this
> case, since I fix it to a constant instead of mapping it to a variable. I
> guess the difference is that, as an aesthetic, it gets passed to the
> underlying stat function. But then, stat_identity does not take any
> arguments...

Yes, this is technically a bug, but it's hard to fix and it crops up
so rarely that I haven't bothered - width is tricky because it
indirectly affects the range of the x axis.

> My problem probably came from not realizing that errorbar is a geom in
> itself, completely independent of whatever you draw underneath. So, if I
> want the two layers to match, I have to deal with the placement myself. I
> guess I was spoiled by the rest of ggplot which usually deals with this kind
> of graphical alignment for you. Plus, error bars are rarely drawn by
> themselves. Conceptually, they often complement another geom rather than
> being a geom per se. So one could expect them to be automatically aligned to
> whatever they complement.

Yes, each layer is completely independent from the others that come
before it, which means that you do need to align them yourself.  It's
very hard to do this in general, and I'm pretty certain it would end
up being a nuisance in other circumstances.

Regards,

Hadley

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm enjoying working with ggplot2, but the most recent upgrade of all my packages, including ggplot2, seems to have broken something. Here's the code that worked in the previous version but now doesn't:

> summary(ef4.LC2)
    Subject     CategoryStructure Instantiation     value           Index
 1      :  16   FFdiff :592       Object:576    Min.   :0.100   Min.   : 1.00
 10     :  16   FFequal:576       Parts :592    1st Qu.:0.600   1st Qu.: 4.75
 11     :  16                                             Median :0.727   Median : 8.50
 12     :  16                                   Mean   :0.732   Mean   : 8.50
 13     :  16                                   3rd Qu.:0.900   3rd Qu.:12.25
 14     :  16                                   Max.   :1.000   Max.   :16.00
 (Other):1072
          Condition
 FFdiff.Object :288
 FFdiff.Parts  :304
 FFequal.Object:288
 FFequal.Parts :288

theme_set(theme_bw())
p <- ggplot(ef4.LC2, aes(Index, value, colour=Condition))
p <- p + stat_summary(fun.data="mean_cl_boot", geom="smooth", size=2, alpha=.1)
p <- p + scale_colour_manual(value=c("darkred", "red", "darkgreen", "green"))
p <- p + scale_x_continuous("Block", breaks=c(1,6,11,16))
p <- p + scale_y_continuous("Mean Accuracy", limits=c(.5,1))
p <- p + opts(plot.margin=unit(c(1,5,2,2), "lines"))
p

When I run the above, I get the following warning:
WARNING: Warning: Removed 116 rows containing missing values (stat_summary).

(There are no missing values in the data.) And the plot is broken, as if the Index was not sorted or something. (See attachment.)

This seems to be an issue with stat_summary or mean_cl_boot, or maybe with Hmisc, I'm not sure. Simpler plots work fine. Any ideas? Thanks,

 -Harlan

messages.subject: Integer treated as continuous
messages.body_plain:
qplot(1,1,colour=1:2) == qplot(1,1,c(1L,2L)) shows a scale for colour including values 1.2, 1.4, 1.6, and 1.8.

But the color can't possibly have those values, since it is integer-valued, not double-valued.

A workaround is to write qplot(1,1,colour=as.factor(1:2) )

Is it intentional that integers are treated as continuous?  It has bitten me a couple of times, where (e.g.) I was using an integer as an experiment number or a subject number.

messages.body_plain:
OK. This is strange. It has something to do maybe with numeric vs ascii sorting or something? I'm attaching an rda file with a subset of my data (8 subjects worth). To reproduce the problem:

> library("ggplot2")

> load("test-8Ss.rda")
> ggplot(head(ef4.LC2,72), aes(Index, value, colour=Condition)) + stat_summary(fun.data="mean_cl_normal", geom="smooth", size=2, alpha=.1)
> ggplot(head(ef4.LC2,80), aes(Index, value, colour=Condition)) + stat_summary(fun.data="mean_cl_normal", geom="smooth", size=2, alpha=.1)

The first ggplot looks fine (error bars are big, of course). Notice the x axis goes to 9. The second ggplot, where the x axis goes to 10 is garbage. There's no obvious problem with the data between rows 72 and 80. The data was put into this format by cast/melt calls. (I had to fill in some missing data.)

The data types seems reasonable -- everything that should be a factor is a factor, and everything that should be numeric is numeric. The order of the rows in the data frame shouldn't matter (right??), but in any case they're in the order of the Index (x) variable.

Thank you for any suggestions!

messages.body_plain:
Hi Folks,

I am pretty new to R and I am even newer to ggplot.

I am using R 2.7.1, 2.8.1, and 2.9.0 on linux host and
what I am experiencing holds for all three.

I was just typing a few examples from the chapter 2 of
the book, ggplot2 --Elegant graphics for data analysis.

I typed 3 qplot lines on page 13:
  > qplot (carat, price, data=diamonds, slpha = i(1/10))
  > qplot (carat, price, data=diamonds, slpha = i(1/100))
  > qplot (carat, price, data=diamonds, slpha = i(1/200))

To me, the plot looked identical.  I went to my R library
directory and looked at the date on the ggplot2 directory,
which was April of 2008.  I decided to update the library.
In R, I issued:
  > install.packages ('ggplot2', '/usr/local/Gallo/R')
and there was a complaint as to permission denied for
saving the current version (or something).  I reissued
the command as root and this time it gave me a normal
return.

I was ready to retrace my steps with the book.  I only got
to page 11 this time.  Here's what happened (in all three
versions):
  > set.seed (1410)
  > dsmall <- diamonds [sample (nrow(diamonds), 100), ]
  >
  > qplot (carat, price, data = diamonds)
  Error in get("new", env = FacetGrid, inherits = TRUE)
(FacetGrid, ...) :
    could not find function "is.formula"
  >

Can somebody please clue me in as to what's happening,
what I am doing wrong, etc?

Regards,

Tena Sakai
tsa...@gallo.ucsf.edu

And you want

not

Hadley

messages.subject: Combining colors
messages.body_plain:
I would like to use color blending to represent overplotting of 2-3 different series more effectively.  Even where points are overplotted to the point where I can't distinguish the individual densities of point type A and point type B, I'd like to visualize the relative density of one or the other.

I've tried experimenting with the subtractive primaries (cyan, magenta, yellow) and alpha blending seems to do something moderately useful here (though yellow is visually much 'lighter' than the other two), but it's not great. I'd think that something like straight color addition (using additive
primaries) instead of alpha-blending might give better results (with the sums renormalized to 1), but I don't really know.

Another problem with the alpha blending trick for single colors is that overplotting has an effective range of 0 to 1/alpha (linearly), which isn't very robust when some areas of the plot are much more heavily overplotted than others.  I wonder if there's some way to make this nonlinear (probit or log or whatever)....

Surely someone has thought about the use of color in overplotting more systematically?

         -s

messages.body_plain:
Here are a couple of examples of what I have in mind:

clump <- function(x0=0,p=.5,n=500,prob=c(p,1-p),vdist=rexp)
  data.frame(x=runif(n,0,1)+x0,
             y=vdist(n),
             c=factor( sample(length(prob),n,prob=prob,replace=TRUE),
                       levels=1:length(prob),
                       ordered=TRUE ))

cc <- rbind(clump(0,0),clump(1,.4),clump(2,.2),clump(3,.6),clump(4,.4),clump(5,1))

dd <- rbind(clump(0,prob=c(.1,.3,.6)),
            clump(1,prob=c(.1,.6,.3)),
            clump(2,prob=c(.3,.1,.6)),
            clump(3,prob=c(.3,.6,.1)),
            clump(4,prob=c(.6,.1,.3)),
            clump(5,prob=c(.6,.3,.1)))

ee <- rbind(clump(0,0,vdist=runif),clump(1,.4,vdist=runif),clump(2,.2,vdist=runif),
            clump(3,.6,vdist=runif),clump(4,.4,vdist=runif),clump(5,1,vdist=runif))

test <- function(data) qplot(x,y,colour=c,data=data,size=I(5),alpha=I(.5))

Now try test(cc), test(dd), test(ee).

To a certain extent, you can see the different proportions through the color, but you have to look fairly hard.  I am imagining that there is some better way of combining colors so that the mixing proportions are more clearly visualized.

             -s

messages.subject: Re: [R] Bumps chart in R
messages.body_plain:
(cross posting to the ggplot2 group for posterity)

Here's how I'd approach it:

library(ggplot2)
text = letters[1:20]
tal1 = rnorm (20,5,2)
tal2 = rnorm (20,6,3)
dif = tal2-tal1
df0 = data.frame(text,tal1,tal2)
df = melt(
	data = df0
	, id.vars = 'text'
	, variable_name = 'tal'
)
df$dif = dif
df$col = ifelse(dif>0,'red',ifelse(dif<0,'blue','black'))
df$size = abs(dif)

# draw the plot
ggplot(
	data=df
	, aes(
		x=tal
		, y=value
		, group=text
	)
) +
geom_line(
	aes(
		size=size
		, colour=col
	)
)+
geom_text(
	aes(
		label=text
	)
)+
opts(
	legend.position="none"
)+
theme_bw()

Unfortunately it's not perfect:
(1) col isn't being interpreted literally, so instead of truly red & blue.
(2) the lines ends are square whereas usually they're rounded.
(3) attempting to remove the legend via opts(legend.position="none")
seems to fail.

messages.subject: RE: [R] Bumps chart in R
messages.body_plain:
Dear Andreas and Mike,

You need to use scale_colour_manual() if you want to set the colours yourself. Ggplot2 interpretes the "col" variable in the dataset as an ordinairy factor.

library(ggplot2)
df0 <- data.frame(text = letters[1:21], tal1 = c(rnorm (20,5,2), 5), tal2 = c(rnorm (20,6,3), 5))
df0$dif <- df0$tal2 - df0$tal1
df <- melt(data = df0, id.vars = c('text', 'dif'), variable_name = 'tal')
df$Change <- factor(ifelse(df$dif>0,'Up',ifelse(df$dif<0,'Down','Stable')), levels = c("Up", "Stable", "Down"))
df$size <- abs(df$dif)
ggplot(df, aes(x = tal, y = value, label = text, group = text, size = size, col = Change)) + geom_line() + geom_text(data = subset(df, tal=="tal1"), size=3, hjust=2, vjust=0) + scale_x_discrete("Change from time to time") + scale_y_continuous("Points") + theme_bw()+ opts(legend.position="none")+ opts(title="As time went by\n") +opts(plot.title=theme_text(vjust=0,size=20)) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("red", "black", "blue"))

HTH,

Thierry

messages.subject: ggplot feedback
messages.body_plain:
Hadley,

ggplot2 is fantastic.  I have gotten amazing things done with it of immediate value to my work, and seen things in my data that I probably wouldn't have simply because it would have been too much trouble to set up the necessary graphs in other systems.

The ggplot2 book is also fantastic -- congratulations again on getting it to the publisher.

I do have some feedback for you on things that could increase ggplot's takeup by new users.  It is easy to focus on cool new features (including ones that I ask for...), more beautiful output, and so on, but there are other matters that are also important to users: error handling, display consistency, and documentation.

First of all, it seems to me that ggplot generally does a poor job of detecting bad input and giving error messages that make sense to users.  If I omit an aes where it wants one, or nest things incorrectly, or misspell something, or have an empty data frame, etc. etc., I usually get internal error messages ("attempt to apply non-function" is a popular one) from routines that ggplot is calling, usually without mentioning what part of the input is incorrect.  Traceback doesn't help; it just shows more *internal* detail.  Even when the error message is meaningful ("undefined columns selected"), it (a) doesn't give the name of the column in question or its context (was it in a facet spec? a group spec? an aes?), and (b) the error comes from an internal call to `[.data.frame` rather than from some part of ggplot.  I realize that handling errors cleanly can often take as much code as handling the correct cases correctly, but that (alas) is the nature of quality software.  I also realize that much other R software shares the same flaw, but it is still a flaw.

Secondly, on-screen display should be identical to output in other output forms (notably pdf).  It is frustrating to create a perfect plot on-screen only to discover that it is illegible on paper (especially since paper has higher resolution...) because legends overlap etc.

Third, the documentation needs to be filled out -- I believe this is already planned.  In the meantime, perhaps the man pages, instead of reading "All documentation is available at <URL: http://had.co.nz/ggplot2>." could point to the specific URL on had.co.nz <http://had.co.nz>.  Also, it would be useful to have some documentation on how the user can write new geom's, new stat's, etc.

Thanks again for a fantastic package.

           -s

messages.subject: Re: Bumps chart in R
messages.body_plain:
Mike

In reply to your comments 1 and 3 below:
(1) add scale_colour_identity() to your script, and it will map the
plot colours to values in the dataframe.

(3) opts(legend.position="none") fails because it is overridden by
theme_bw(), which specifies that the legend should be on the right-
hand side. Change their order in the script, so that theme_bw() is
called before opts(legend.position="none"), and the plot will have no
legend.

--
http://learnr.wordpress.com/

It does indeed: since you split them by colour, it considers it
different data groups (see plot on p31 of the ggplot book and the
grouping section).

In that case you need to switch to the ggplot construct and have some
explicit geom calls with independent aes. Something along the lines of:

ggplot(joks) + geom_point(aes(x=days, y=grass_1, colour=Patient_Name))
+ geom_smooth(aes(x=days, y=grass_1)) +

scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(188, 371, 554, 737), labels =
c("Jan","July", "Jan", "July", "Jan"))

But indeed a minimal example, with data, would help.

NB: I spelled the aes calls completely for each geom for clarity but
you can keep the common ones in gggplot:

ggplot(joks, ares(x=days, y=grass_1)) +
geom_point(aes(colour=Patient_Name)) + geom_smooth() +

scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(188, 371, 554, 737), labels =
c("Jan","July", "Jan", "July", "Jan"))

messages.subject: numbers at risk on kaplan-meier curve
messages.subject_clean: numbers at risk on kaplan-meier curve
messages.body_plain:
I've been tweaking some lines, from a thread a few weeks ago, trying to
get a decent kaplan-meier curve with numbers at risk printed below the
x-axis.

Two things I'd welcome suggestions on (1) lining up the numbers at risk
with the time points on the k-m curve - it doesn't look to bad on the
screen, but doesn't look right when saved as a pdf and (2) there's a
white box around the legend which I can't seem to figure out how to
remove - unless there are other suggestions to prettify the legend.

I'm trying to generalise as much as possible and minimise on data
dependent tweaking so that the code would be useable with minimal
changes for different datasets.

Thanks

Gary

The code to reproduce the figure is

library(ggplot2)
require(survival)

fit <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ rx, data = colon)

df <- data.frame(
   time    = fit$time,
   n.risk  = fit$n.risk,
   n.event = fit$n.event,
   surv    = fit$surv,
   strata  = gsub("rx=", "", summary(fit, censored = T)$strata),
   upper   = fit$upper,
   lower   = fit$lower
)

zeros <- data.frame(time = 0, surv = 1, strata = gsub("rx=", "",
levels(summary(fit)$strata)), upper = 1, lower = 1)

df <- rbind.fill(zeros, df)

p <- ggplot(df, aes(time, surv, colour = strata)) +
	geom_step(size = 0.6) +
	xlim(0, max(fit$time)) +
	ylim(0, 1) +
	xlab("days from randomization") +
	ylab("survival probability") +
	scale_colour_brewer(name = "Treatment", pal = "Set1") +
	opts(legend.position = c(0.9, 0.9)) +
	opts(legend.key = theme_rect(colour = NA))

times <- seq(0, max(fit$time), by = 500)

risk.data <- data.frame(strata = summary(fit, times = times, extend =
T)$strata,
     time = summary(fit, times = times, extend = T)$time,
     n.risk = summary(fit, times = times, extend = T)$n.risk)

data_table <- ggplot(risk.data, aes(x = time, y = strata, label =
format(n.risk, nsmall = 0)), colour = strata) +
     geom_text(size = 3.5) +
     theme_bw() +
     scale_y_discrete(formatter = abbreviate, limits = c("rx=Obs",
"rx=Lev", "rx=Lev+5FU"), labels = c("Obs", "Lev", "Lev+5FU")) +
     opts(panel.grid.major = theme_blank()) +
     opts(panel.grid.minor = theme_blank()) +
     opts(panel.border     = theme_blank()) +
     opts(axis.text.x      = theme_blank()) +
     opts(axis.ticks       = theme_blank()) +
     xlim(0, max(fit$time))

data_table <- data_table + opts(legend.position = "none") + xlab(NULL) +
ylab(NULL)

data_table <- data_table + opts(plot.margin = unit(c(-0.5, 0, 0, -0.75),
"lines"))

# + opts(plot.margin = unit(c(-0.5, 1, 0, 0.5), "lines")) + xlab(NULL) +
ylab(NULL)

Layout <- grid.layout(nrow = 2, ncol = 1,heights = unit (c(2, .25),
c("null", "null")))

vplayout <- function (...) {
     grid.newpage()
     pushViewport(viewport(layout = Layout))
}

subplot <- function(x, y) viewport(layout.pos.row = x, layout.pos.col = y)
mmplot <- function(a, b) {
     vplayout()
     print(a, vp = subplot(1, 1))
     print(b, vp = subplot(2, 1))
}

#pdf("c:\\test.pdf", pointsize=11, paper="a4r", width=10, height=10)
mmplot(p, data_table)
#dev.off()

messages.subject: Re: Multiple rugs
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

It seems hard-coded, but you could slightly modify the geom and create your own like this,

GeomRug <- proto(Geom, {
  draw <- function(., data, scales, coordinates, ...) {
    rugs <- list()
    data <- coordinates$transform(data, scales)
    if (!is.null(data$x)) {
      rugs$x <- with(data, segmentsGrob(
        x0 = unit(x, "native"), x1 = unit(x, "native"),
        y0 = unit(ystart, "npc"), y1 = unit(ystart, "npc") + unit(ylen, "npc"),  # FIRST MODIF
        gp = gpar(col = alpha(colour, alpha), lty = linetype, lwd = size * .pt)
      ))
    }

    if (!is.null(data$y)) {
      rugs$y <- with(data, segmentsGrob(
        y0 = unit(y, "native"), y1 = unit(y, "native"),
        x0 = unit(xstart, "npc"), x1 = unit(xstart, "npc") + unit(xlen, "npc"),  # SECOND MODIF
        gp = gpar(col = alpha(colour, alpha), lty = linetype, lwd = size * .pt)
      ))
    }

    gTree(children = do.call("gList", rugs))
  }

  objname <- "rug"

  desc <- "Free rug plots"

  default_stat <- function(.) StatIdentity

  default_aes <- function(.) # THIRD MODIF
        aes(colour="black", size=0.5, linetype=1, alpha = 1, ystart=0, ylen=0.03, xstart=0, xlen=0.03)
  guide_geom <- function(.) "path"

  examples <- function(.) {
    p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=wt, y=mpg))
    p + geom_point()
    p + geom_point() + geom_rug()
    p + geom_point() + geom_rug(position='jitter')
  }

})

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=wt, y=mpg))

p + geom_point() + geom_rug()
p + geom_point() + geom_rug(xstart=0.5)

I'm not sure how to rename it as a new geom though, and it would need some thoughts about stacking several rugs on top of each other automatically (whether that's a good idea or not I dunno).

HTH,

baptiste

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm also interested in getting axes to align via Grid, but as far as I
know your best option is to create a dummy facetting variable instead.
Try this,

x <- seq(1992, 2002, by=2)

d1 <- data.frame(x=x, y=rnorm(length(x)))

xy <- expand.grid(x=x, y=x)
d2 <- data.frame(x=xy$x, y=xy$y, z= jitter(xy$x + xy$y))

d1$panel <- "a"
d2$panel <- "b"
d1$z <- d1$x # dummy to match the number of columns

d <- rbind(d1, d2) # d is not really necessary in fact

ggplot(data = d, mapping = aes(x = x, y = y)) +
facet_grid(panel~., scale="free") +
layer(data= d1,  geom = c( "line"), stat = "identity" ) + # each layer
can have its own data
layer(data=d2, mapping=aes(colour=z, fill=z),  geom = c( "tile"), stat
= "identity" )

Instead of a global y label, you may want to use the strips to provide
a different label for each plot.

HTH,

baptiste

messages.subject: How to alter the order of the keys in a legend?
messages.subject_clean: How to alter the order of the keys in a legend?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

How can I alter the order of the keys in a legend of a stacked
barchart? I've tried to use "Branche" as a ordered factor, but it
doesn't work:

factor(c(rep("Textil",6),rep("Metall/Maschinen",6),rep("Uhren",6),rep
("Chemie/Pharmazie",6),rep("Nahrungsmittel",6),rep("Andere",6)),
ordered=TRUE)

With this factor it works, but it isn't very elegant:

factor(c(rep("a_Textil",6),rep("b_Metall/Maschinen",6),rep("c_Uhren",
6),rep("d_Chemie/Pharmazie",6),rep("e_Nahrungsmittel",6),rep
("f_Andere",6)), ordered=TRUE)

My barchart:
q<-ggplot(k, aes(x=Jahr, y=Export, fill=Branche))
r<- q + layer(
geom="bar",
position="stack",
stat_params = list(binwidth = 1)
)
r

Thanks a lot.
Ruedi

messages.subject: Re: ggplot feedback
messages.body_plain:
> ggplot2 is fantastic.  I have gotten amazing things done with it of
> immediate value to my work, and seen things in my data that I probably
> wouldn't have simply because it would have been too much trouble to set up
> the necessary graphs in other systems.

Thanks :)

> I do have some feedback for you on things that could increase ggplot's
> takeup by new users.  It is easy to focus on cool new features (including
> ones that I ask for...), more beautiful output, and so on, but there are
> other matters that are also important to users: error handling, display
> consistency, and documentation.

I totally agree with all these points.  Unfortunately I am basically
employed to do research, and while I think what I do with ggplot2 is
of value to the wider statistics community, it's going to be hard to
sell to my tenure committee.  This means I basically have to do
ggplot2 development in my own time, making sure I keep producing and
publishing novel research.

> First of all, it seems to me that ggplot generally does a poor job of
> detecting bad input and giving error messages that make sense to users.  If
> I omit an aes where it wants one, or nest things incorrectly, or misspell
> something, or have an empty data frame, etc. etc., I usually get internal
> error messages ("attempt to apply non-function" is a popular one) from
> routines that ggplot is calling, usually without mentioning what part of the
> input is incorrect.  Traceback doesn't help; it just shows more *internal*
> detail.  Even when the error message is meaningful ("undefined columns
> selected"), it (a) doesn't give the name of the column in question or its
> context (was it in a facet spec? a group spec? an aes?), and (b) the error
> comes from an internal call to `[.data.frame` rather than from some part of
> ggplot.  I realize that handling errors cleanly can often take as much code
> as handling the correct cases correctly, but that (alas) is the nature of
> quality software.  I also realize that much other R software shares the same
> flaw, but it is still a flaw.

If you could provide a large set of such problems then I could spend a
couple of hours and make many improvements to error reporting, rather
than attacking them piece-by-piece as I do now.

> Secondly, on-screen display should be identical to output in other output
> forms (notably pdf).  It is frustrating to create a perfect plot on-screen
> only to discover that it is illegible on paper (especially since paper has
> higher resolution...) because legends overlap etc.

Some of this is out of my control - rendering a plot on disk should
produce identical output to on-screen, so when it doesn't happen it
usually reflects a bug in base R.  Such bugs really need to be
reported up stream, so minimal reproducible examples really help, as
well as the time and energy (and thick skin) required to shepherd the
bug through r-devel to actually get a fix.

> Third, the documentation needs to be filled out -- I believe this is already
> planned.  In the meantime, perhaps the man pages, instead of reading "All
> documentation is available at <URL: http://had.co.nz/ggplot2>." could point

There shouldn't be any of these left - but it's quite possible there
are :(  ggplot2 documentation should be the most accessible area for
actually contributing patches.

> to the specific URL on had.co.nz <http://had.co.nz>.  Also, it would be useful to have some
> documentation on how the user can write new geom's, new stat's, etc.

I've made some efforts on this in the past, but it's a lot of work,
because I need to describe more of the internals of ggplot, which
still aren't completely fixed.  (Especially when I start writing about
them and realise a better way to do it).

Hadley

--

messages.subject: Re: Combining colors
messages.body_plain:
> To a certain extent, you can see the different proportions through the
> color, but you have to look fairly hard.  I am imagining that there is some
> better way of combining colors so that the mixing proportions are more
> clearly visualized.

I agree, but I'm not aware of anything in the literature.

To tackle this problem in general, it's probably best to do a 2d
density estimate yourself (on a common grid), and then compute and
visualise various quantities of interest.  For example, plot f_a -
f_b, or f_a / (f_a + f_b).

Colour mixing will probably work for 2 or 3 colours, but it will
become increasingly hard to separate out the different colours.

I have some very preliminary ideas along these lines for a paper, but
I haven't made much progress.

Hadley

--

messages.subject: Re: Combining colors
messages.body_plain:
Agreed that 3 factor levels is probably the limit for this technique,
since the human visual system basically has 3 independent color
variables.

My own very preliminary idea would assign an additive primary (R, G,
B) to each level and have overplotting correspond to color addition,
with a final normalization step.  Even better if the dots were fuzzy,
making it a sort of kernel relative density calculation.

messages.subject: Re: How to alter the order of the keys in a legend?
messages.subject_clean: How to alter the order of the keys in a legend?
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Hadley, thanks to Xie Chao!
At last, I've found a solution by xavier.chardon at rennes.inra.fr <http://rennes.inra.fr>
that works.
The example with the data I've sent yesterday follows.
Kind regards
Ruedi

#package
library(ggplot2)

#read data
zwila<-data.frame(read.table("data.txt"
, header=TRUE, sep="", na.strings="NA", dec=".", strip.white=TRUE))
colnames(zwila)<-c("Jahr", "Branche", "Export")

#theme

ep_theme <- theme_update(
axis.text.x = theme_text( colour='grey50'),
axis.text.y = theme_text(hjust=1, colour='grey50'),
panel.grid.major = theme_line(colour='grey80'),
panel.grid.minor = theme_line(colour='grey80'),

axis.ticks = theme_blank(),
legend.position =c(0.30,0.79))

#Solution of xavier.chardon at rennes.inra.fr <http://rennes.inra.fr>
#res$f1 <- factor(res$f1, levels = unique(res$f1) )
#with f1 sorted in the order you want it to appear.

zwila$Branche <- factor(zwila$Branche, levels = unique(zwila
$Branche))

q<-ggplot(zwila, aes(x=Jahr, y=Export, fill=Branche))

r<- q + layer(
geom="bar",
position="stack",
stat_params = list(binwidth = 1)
)
r

messages.body_plain:
I have decided to learn ggplot- so therefore this; my first post in
the dedicated ggplot2 group.

I would like to reproduce something similar to this (QOLI report by
M.Frisch): http://wana.dk/wp-content/uploads/2009/05/plot_to_reproduce.png

But how? - Below what I got so far for one of them.

# The data
Health <- -4#
Self-esteem <- -6#
Self_esteem <- -6#
Goals_Values <- 4#
Money <- -3#
Children <- 0#
test <- data.frame(Self_esteem,Goals_Values,Money,Children)#
row.names(test) <- "score"#
t1 <- melt(test)#

messages.subject: Problems with factors
messages.body_plain:
There seem to be various problems with factors in ggplot....

1) ggplot ignores factor ordering

df <- data.frame(
          a=factor(c("r","y","o","l","a"),levels=letters,ordered=T),
          b=factor(c("l","s","q","b","a"),levels=letters,ordered=T))

ggplot(df) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=b))

gives a diagonal line.

2) ggplot does not understand ranges in factors

ggplot(df) +  geom_point(aes(x=a,y=b)) +
geom_rect(aes(x=a,y=b),xmin="y",xmax="l",ymin="s",ymax="b")

Error in x - from[1] : non-numeric argument to binary operator

Though it allows using their scaled positions (not their as.integer values):

ggplot(df) +  geom_point(aes(x=a,y=b)) +
geom_rect(aes(x=a,y=b),xmin=2,xmax=4,ymin=2,ymax=4)

3) geom_path doesn't work with factors

ggplot(df) +  geom_path(aes(x=a,y=b))

produces the plot background, but nothing in it.

>
> gives a diagonal line.

Works for me - do you have the latest version of ggplot2 installed?

> 2) ggplot does not understand ranges in factors
>
> ggplot(df) +  geom_point(aes(x=a,y=b)) +
> geom_rect(aes(x=a,y=b),xmin="y",xmax="l",ymin="s",ymax="b")

That's a bug, but it's pretty easy to work around:

ggplot(df) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=b)) +
geom_rect(aes(x=a,y=b,xmin="y",xmax="l",ymin="s",ymax="b"))

> 3) geom_path doesn't work with factors
>
> ggplot(df) +  geom_path(aes(x=a,y=b))
>
> produces the plot background, but nothing in it.

You need to understand the grouping rules:

 ggplot(df) +  geom_path(aes(x=a,y=b, group = 1))

By default a group is created for each combination of discrete
variables in the plot.  95% of the time this is what you want -
however, when you have discrete position variables you often need to
override this default.

Hadley

messages.subject: Fully specified geom still requires aes?
messages.subject_clean: Fully specified geom still requires aes?
messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure I understand something very basic in ggplot.

Each geom's parameters can be either mapped to a variable or set
directly.  But it seems that ggplot requires a mapping even if the
parameters are fully specified by setting and the parameters are
ignored. Why is that?

For example:

df <- data.frame(
     Domain = factor(rev(c("Health","Self-Esteem","Goals &
Values","Money","Work","Play")),ordered=TRUE),
     Satisfaction = c(  -4, -6, 4, -3, -2, -2 ) )

This gives an error (No data to plot):

ggplot(df) +
  geom_rect(xmin=-6.5,xmax=-3  ,ymin=-100,ymax=100,fill=gray(.3)) +
  geom_point(data=df,aes(x=Satisfaction,y=Domain),size=5,shape=15)

even though every parameter needed to plot the rect is given.

But this works:

ggplot(df) +
  geom_rect(aes(x=Satisfaction,y=Domain),xmin=-6.5,xmax=-3
,ymin=-100,ymax=100,fill=gray(.3)) +   # add aes
  geom_point(data=df,aes(x=Satisfaction,y=Domain),size=5,shape=15)

even though the values of x and y defined in the aes are ignored.

messages.body_plain:
On Sat, May 9, 2009 at 5:17 PM, Stavros Macrakis <macr...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I'm not sure I understand something very basic in ggplot.
>
> Each geom's parameters can be either mapped to a variable or set
> directly.  But it seems that ggplot requires a mapping even if the
> parameters are fully specified by setting and the parameters are
> ignored. Why is that?

This is one of the reasons why coming up with good error messages in
ggplot2 is so hard.  This is perfectly valid plot specification (if a
little unusual) but because I tried to come up with an informative
error message when you didn't specify any data, I broke this case.
(The true situation is a little bit more complicated, iirc, because
some of the manipulations performed to the data when faceting require
a data frame, but this is essentially a implementation problem)

You might want to have a look at the annotate function that wraps up
this common pattern in a way that will work reliably.  Your example
would become:

+ annotate("rect", xmin=-6.5,xmax=-3  ,ymin=-100,ymax=100,fill=gray(.3))

This is slightly shorter, and hopefully reflects the intent of that
line (to add an annotation) more clearly.  If you look at the source
code of annotate you'll see it works by creating a data frame for the
position aesthetics - these are the only aesthetics that are
guaranteed to be present for every geom.

Regards,

Hadley

Hi,

it could be one of several things i suppose:

- visual artifact of the image viewer (such Moiré is typical of images
displayed in pdf viewers) --- but here you seem to use quartz so it
should not happen, i think

- you have set the colour of the tiles to the grey value (or perhaps
NA as grey is the default background). Try to set colour = "your
variable" in addition to fill = "your variable" in the aes() call.
Actually, after testing on a dummy example, it seems that you'd be
better off not specifying colour at all in aes() for some reason that
I don't really understand. Try both, then :). And it may be that the
type of your colour variable matters (factor or numeric?...)

- your data has some weird pattern in it (in which case, try to give a
reproducible example), at least str("your data.frame")

- perhaps something else

I'm guessing it's # 2

HTH,

baptiste

Here's one attempt:

bg <- data.frame(
  start = c(-6.5, -3, -0.5, 0.5),
  end = c(-3, -0.5, 0.5, 6.5),
  fill = grey(c(0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.8))

  # Data points

  scale_x_continuous("Domain", limits=c(-6.5,6.5), expand = c(0,0)) +

  # first layer pretends it is continuous

  # Just treat the background fill as a fill - don't scale it

  opts(panel.grid.major = theme_blank())

Well, by that argument, "Health" or "Auckland" or whatever other value
of a factor/string is just as meaningful in the context of the plot,
isn't it? And is unambiguous as an x/y coordinate.

The problem comes when the aesthetic space and the data space can be
of the same class.  Shape, for example, is specified using a number
and colour is specified using a string. (Why don't they have their own
classes? Presumably because of tradition and convenience....)

Arguably xmin in setting context should be in aesthetic space (whether
that is 0.0 - 1.0 as the edges of the plot space or pixel number 1-400
or 0.0-2.3 inches or whatever), but that doesn't seem terribly useful.

             -s

messages.subject: More glitches/questions
messages.body_plain:
A few more questions/glitches/possible misunderstandings....

* Here's a difference between mapped and set values -- I don't know if
it is by design.  It seems that set values do not affect the scale's
range calculation, while mapped ones do:

  ggplot(data.frame(x=0:1,y=0:1)) +
  geom_rect(aes(x=x,y=y,ymin=-3),xmin=.1,xmax=.2,ymax=3000)

has a y-range of -3 .. 1 (ignoring the 3000).

* About annotate, I couldn't find it in the book -- I guess it's new with 0.8.3?

Unlike 'set' values, annotate values *do* affect the range
calculation, which makes them less handy/useful in the case of
background rectangles defining zones.  How can I get them auto-clipped
to the display area?

* On the other hand, if the set y-range (which doesn't affect ranges)
is infinite (I did this not because I was testing corner cases but
because it was the logical thing to do when the band does not have any
vertical limits), no rectangle is plotted at all:

   ggplot(data.frame(x=0:1,y=0:1)) +
   geom_rect(aes(x=x,y=y),xmin=.1,xmax=.2,ymin=-Inf,ymax=Inf)

* It appears that xlim cancels the effect of scale...log10:

 ggplot(ddd) + geom_line(aes(x=x,y=y)) + xlim(1,3)+ scale_x_log10()
# log scale, limits set
 ggplot(ddd) + geom_line(aes(x=x,y=y)) + scale_x_log10() + xlim(1,3)
# linear scale, limits set

In the first case, the changes to the scale are cumulative; in the
second, xlim cancels log10, as though it had an implicit linear scale.
 Is this intentional? Is it documented?

* In the case of size, mapped sizes are (very reasonably) scaled by
the system.  'Set' sizes seem to scale as some sort of proportion of
the plotted range; is the behavior documented somewhere?

# Light grey lines appear
# -------------------------------

x<-1:87
y<-1:61
xy<-expand.grid(x=x,y=y)
d1 <- data.frame(x=x, y=rnorm(length(x)))
d2<-data.frame(x=xy$x,y=xy$y,z=as.vector(t(data)))

d1$panel <- "a"
d2$panel <- "c"

d1$z <- d1$x

d <- rbind(d1,d2)

p <- ggplot(data=d, mapping=aes(x = x,y = y))
p <- p + facet_grid(panel~.,scale="free")
p <- p + layer(data=d1, geom=c("line"), stat = "identity")
p <- p + layer(data=d2, mapping=aes(colour=z, fill=z), geom=c("tile"),
stat = "identity")

p

# ---------------------------------------------------------

The problem seems to arise when you specify both colour and fill in

d<- t(volcano)[ncol(volcano):1,]

I'm not sure why this behaviour is observed, it may have something to
do with the linewidth of the squares that is slightly too thin to
merge the neighbouring elements together.

Anyway, if you don't need it, just remove colour in aes().

messages.subject: Re: creating a new geom
messages.body_plain:
Great idea - thanks for doing this!

> It's almost there for the geom part, but I'm struggling with mapping
> and recycling rules. I generalised my initial idea of ellipses to
> regular polygons with arbitrary number of sides (3 to 12, and 50 for
> smooth paths).

What in particular are you having problems with?  I can see a couple
of things that you could change for better compatibility with the rest
of ggplot2:

 * use angle instead of theta
 * make sure size is interpreted in mm
 * when a geom has both colour and fill, alpha should be applied to the fill

I can also see that you'll need some new scales:

 * scale_angle should scale to 0, 2 pi
 * scale_sides should be a discrete scale
 * I'm not sure about the aspect ratio

You'll also need to implement draw_legend eventually, but that should
be pretty simple.

Hadley

> Thanks for the tips. It's not as hard as first feared, although i can > see how taking care of all the details and produce a robust code > could be a nightmare! Yes, the basics are pretty easy - it's all the edge cases that are hard. > say, I want to map the color of the diamonds to the number of sides of > a polygon, > > > dsmall <- diamonds[sample(nrow(diamonds), 100), ] > d <- ggplot(dsmall, aes(carat, price)) > str(dsmall) > d + geom_ngon(aes(fill = carat, sides=as.numeric(color)), > colour="orange",ar=1, size=5, angle=pi/3) > > This works, but I shouldn't need as.numeric, and it should also work > for numeric values that are not directly equal to the number of sides > (say, non-integer values as opposed to factor codes). I'm missing a > mapping function somewhere, with different methods for factors, > integers, numeric values. I'm not sure where this transformation > should be written? So this brings you to the next type of ggplot2 object you might want to create - scales. You basically want to create scale_sides_discrete and scale_sides_continuous to deal with two of the possible types of data. > ScaleSides <- proto(ScaleDiscrete, expr={ > doc <- TRUE > common <- NULL > .input <- .output <- "sides" > > output_set <- function(.) c("3", "4", "5", "6", "7", "8", > "0")[seq_along(.$input_set())] > max_levels <- function(.) 9 > > detail <- "

" > > # Documentation ----------------------------------------------- > > objname <- "sides" > desc <- "Scale for polygon sides" > > icon <- function(.) { > # > } > > examples <- function() { > # > # See scale_manual for more flexibility > } > > }) Again, you'll need scale_sides <- ScaleSide$build_accessor() When adding a default scale (e.g. when you use sides as an aesthetic), ggplot2 categorises the type of data into date, datetime, continuous and discrete. It then looks for (e.g.) a scale named scale_sides_discrete or scale_sides_continuous. If it doesn't find a particular type of scale, it uses the generic, scale_sides. So if you want different behaviour for continuous and discrete values, then you need to create scale_sides_continuous and scale_sides_discrete. Hadley -- http://had.co.nz/

messages.subject: Re: More glitches/questions
messages.body_plain:
> * Here's a difference between mapped and set values -- I don't know if
> it is by design.  It seems that set values do not affect the scale's
> range calculation, while mapped ones do:
>
>  ggplot(data.frame(x=0:1,y=0:1)) +
>  geom_rect(aes(x=x,y=y,ymin=-3),xmin=.1,xmax=.2,ymax=3000)
>
> has a y-range of -3 .. 1 (ignoring the 3000).

Yes, again because it's the scales that control the range of the axes,
and scales never see the set values.  I'm not sure whether this is an
appealing feature or not, but it's unlikely to change.

> * About annotate, I couldn't find it in the book -- I guess it's new with 0.8.3?

Yes.

> Unlike 'set' values, annotate values *do* affect the range
> calculation, which makes them less handy/useful in the case of
> background rectangles defining zones.  How can I get them auto-clipped
> to the display area?

Oh, hmmm, I hadn't thought about that. You could just the maximum and
minimum ranges of the data?  And then use expand = c(0,0) in the x and
y scales.

> * On the other hand, if the set y-range (which doesn't affect ranges)
> is infinite (I did this not because I was testing corner cases but
> because it was the logical thing to do when the band does not have any
> vertical limits), no rectangle is plotted at all:
>
>   ggplot(data.frame(x=0:1,y=0:1)) +
>   geom_rect(aes(x=x,y=y),xmin=.1,xmax=.2,ymin=-Inf,ymax=Inf)

I suspect this is due to how the rectangles are drawn by grid.  I'll
look into it.

> * It appears that xlim cancels the effect of scale...log10:
>
>  ggplot(ddd) + geom_line(aes(x=x,y=y)) + xlim(1,3)+ scale_x_log10()
> # log scale, limits set
>  ggplot(ddd) + geom_line(aes(x=x,y=y)) + scale_x_log10() + xlim(1,3)
> # linear scale, limits set
>
> In the first case, the changes to the scale are cumulative; in the
> second, xlim cancels log10, as though it had an implicit linear scale.
>  Is this intentional? Is it documented?

Currently xlim(1,3) is just a short cut for scale_x_continuous(limits
= c(1,3)) which would be overridden by scale_x_log10. (Although the
order shouldn't matter - I don't know why you'd be seeing a
difference).  I have plans to implement xlim in a different way, which
would overcome this problem.

> * In the case of size, mapped sizes are (very reasonably) scaled by
> the system.  'Set' sizes seem to scale as some sort of proportion of
> the plotted range; is the behavior documented somewhere?

Set sizes are in mm.  This should be documented in the specifications
appendix of the book.

Hadley

> isn't it? And is unambiguous as an x/y coordinate.

Yes, you could make that argument.  However, it isn't the way ggplot2
works currently and it's unlikely to change.  Getting categorical
scales right is hard enough as it is.

> The problem comes when the aesthetic space and the data space can be
> of the same class.  Shape, for example, is specified using a number
> and colour is specified using a string. (Why don't they have their own
> classes? Presumably because of tradition and convenience....)

> that is 0.0 - 1.0 as the edges of the plot space or pixel number 1-400
> or 0.0-2.3 inches or whatever), but that doesn't seem terribly useful.

Actually it would be useful - because then you could easily pin geoms
to positions relative to the plot border.  I'm not really sure why it
doesn't work this way already - I'll look into it.

I'm still not sure what to do about geoms with no data (e.g.
geom_rect(xmin = 0, ymin = 0, xmax = 1, ymax = 1).  I know I looked
into this a couple of weeks ago and decided it was too hard to make it
work, but maybe I just didn't have a compelling enough reason to make
it work.

messages.body_plain:
On Fri, May 1, 2009 at 6:14 PM, JiHO <jo.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hello everyone,
>
> I want to draw a circle on top of a ggplot. The circle is of known
> diameter measured in the same dimensions as the axes (everything is in
> cm).
>
> I don't want to "cheat" with solution such as drawing a open circle
> symbol of very large size, or approximating the circle with a
> geom_path. So I figure the way to do it is to dive into grid and
> modify stuff in the guts of the plot. However I have a problem of
> scales:
>
>
> # produce the base plot
> qplot(0,0) + xlim(-5,5) + ylim(-5,5)
>
> # examine the viewport stack
> grid.ls <http://grid.ls>(viewport=T)
> current.vpTree()
> # at that point, I can see that the data point is in panel-3-3
> # Q.1: is there any easy/foolproof way to get that programatically?

No.  I'm hoping this will be easier post layout system rewrite.

> # draw stuff
> grid.circle(0,0,0.5)
> # but these coordinates are relative to the bottom left of the window,
> while I want the circule to be drawn relative to the scales of the
> current plot. According to chapter 5 of the grid book (p.160), I sould
> do:
> grid.circle(0,0,0.5, default.units="native")
> # but this does not work
> # Q. 2: what am I missing here?

Unfortunately ggplot2 doesn't use native scales - by the time the data
gets to the panel, it's been converted to npc type values.  I did use
native scales previously, but it just ends up being easier to do it
all myself.  Unfortunately this results in your problem where you
can't place grid objects relative to the data.  I haven't come up with
a good solution to this - in principle you should be able to save the
information used to render the plot and then re-use it for your own
calculations.

Hadley

messages.subject: Issues with geom_density: closed curve problems
messages.subject_clean: Issues with geom_density: closed curve problems
messages.body_plain:
geom_density plots the density curve but also a horizontal line (y=0);
it also always forces the curve to go through (x=0,y=0), all
apparently to form a closed curve (why?).  This is a fairly minor
annoyance:

     ggplot(data.frame(a=rexp(1000))) + geom_density(aes(x=a))

But if we put the density on a logarithmic scale, the closing line is
at the top of the graph and looks terrible:

     ggplot(data.frame(a=rexp(1000))) + geom_density(aes(x=a)) + scale_y_log10()

Especially ugly when the curve goes above the axis:

    ggplot(data.frame(a=c(rep(1,1000),rexp(1000)))) +
geom_density(aes(x=a)) + scale_y_log10()

Also, using scale limits results in rather poor results:

    set.seed(1); dd <- data.frame(a=c(rep(1,10000),rexp(1000)))
    ggplot(dd) + geom_density(aes(x=a)) + scale_y_log10(limits=c(1e-3,1))

The slicing-off at the top and bottom isn't clean (the line continues
where it should have disappeared, and the line isn't horizontal) and
the "return" line around to the right is a function of where exactly
the distribution was cut off, which is awful.

Somewhat better is to use coord_ to limit the graph:

    ggplot(dd) + geom_density(aes(x=a)) +
scale_y_log10(breaks=10^seq(-2,1,by=.5)) +
coord_cartesian(ylim=c(-2,1))

but this still leaves the "return" line on the left, middle, and
right. (as well as being inconvenient since the coord limits are in
log space, not in data space; and because the scale breaks aren't
calculated automatically for this zoom level).

            -s

messages.body_plain:
> On a side note I was looking at the grImport package and the
> my.symbols function from TeachingDemos --- there might be some
> inspiration for a new geom (admittedly for fairly specific purposes).
> I wonder whether it would be possible to have a geom take an arbitrary
> grob as an argument passed to the draw function (better yet, a
> function creating a new grob).

Yes, but it couldn't be an aesthetic (unless you want to create a
scale that maps from a data value to a function!).  Just do:

 draw <- function(., data, scales, coordinates, customGrob = pointsGrob, ...) {

  with(coordinates$transform(data, scales),
    ggname(.$my_name(),
customGrob(x, y, size, col=alpha(colour, alpha), ...))
  )
 }

and leave it out of the aesthetics.  That makes customGrob a parameter
of the geom.

I have two other similar geoms on my to do list:

* geom_ellipse and matching stat_normal_ellipse similar to
car::data.ellipse.  But how should the ellipse be parameterised?  x,
y, a, b, angle? xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax, angle? centre, cov?

* sunflowers, e.g. http://www.stata.com/meeting/3nasug/sunflower.pdf

messages.body_plain:
On Tue, May 12, 2009 at 2:51 PM, Hadley Wickham <had...@rice.edu> wrote:
>> On a side note I was looking at the grImport package and the
>> my.symbols function from TeachingDemos --- there might be some
>> inspiration for a new geom (admittedly for fairly specific purposes).
>> I wonder whether it would be possible to have a geom take an arbitrary
>> grob as an argument passed to the draw function (better yet, a
>> function creating a new grob).
>

> Yes, but it couldn't be an aesthetic (unless you want to create a
> scale that maps from a data value to a function!).

Well, both are quite exciting ideas for two complementary scenarios,

1) for kids who want little snoopy characters instead of boring
symbols in a plot (everyone knows kids like to attend scientific
conferences). For a grown-ups presentation, you may have to represent
data where the peanuts characters correspond to factors (snoopy,
charlie brown, etc.). Here you'll need a function that selects the
appropriate grob for each level, but these can all be hard-coded in
advance.

2) the my.symbols example (TeachingDemos) with a function passed as a
symbol: here each symbol is a little sparkline graph that needs to be
created from the data.

Another case is the sunflower plot that seems to require a different
grob for each number of observations: it could also fit in this second
scheme to prevent the user from having to create a new geom for each
new idea.

> I have two other similar geoms on my to do list:
>
> * geom_ellipse and matching stat_normal_ellipse similar to
> car::data.ellipse.  But how should the ellipse be parameterised?  x,
> y, a, b, angle? xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax, angle? centre, cov?
>
> * sunflowers, e.g. http://www.stata.com/meeting/3nasug/sunflower.pdf
>

Both of these seem quite similar in form to the geom I started
yesterday: the ellipses I implemented as a 50-edges polygon (example
attached), while the sunflower plot could correspond to a starred
version of the convex polygons (I saw a similar function in the
?my.symbols page).

As for the ellipse, I'm biased towards a parametrisation of the form,

x,y, aspect ratio a/b , angle

but that's probably because I had to implement it in this form in a
base plot once. Note that in the end I chose to have the aspect ratio
preserve the area of the ellipse so that it remains an orthogonal
setting to the size parameter.

Some people (ellipse package I think) seem to prefer the statistician
perspective of a covariance matrix. I guess it doesn't matter if one
provides an example of the conversion from one to another. I can see
difficulties with my parametrisation when one wants to draw this,

http://weitaiyun.blogspot.com/2009/03/visulization-of-correlation-matrix.html

but then again the size could be adjusted to compensate for the aspect
ratio so that the enclosing square remains constant (admittedly i'd
have to think a little bit to get this one right!)

Here's what I've got for ellipses so far,

# ellipse example (no legend yet)

dsmall <- diamonds[sample(nrow(diamonds), 100), ]
d <- ggplot(dsmall, aes(carat, price))
str(dsmall)
library(ggplotpp)

d + geom_ngon(aes(colour = carat, angle = x, ar=y), fill=NA,  sides=50)

messages.subject: line plot to visualize three-way lm interaction
messages.subject_clean: line plot to visualize three-way lm interaction
messages.body_plain:
Hello again, thanks for your help on my earlier problem, I now have
another one!  Sorry to not include reproducible code this time.

I am running across the situation of having to interpret three-way
regression interactions graphically.... I am interested in your
thoughts on the best/easiest way to use ggplot() for the scenario
below:

With one continuous dependent variable Y and three continuous
predictors x1, x2, x3, assume the lm call (Y ~ x1*x2*x3) is run and
results in a significant three-way interaction.  I am interested in a
line plot that evaluates the regression model at arbitrary "low" (-1
SD) and "high" (+1 SD) values of each predictor variable, to create a
somewhat quick-and-dirty method for exploring such interactions
graphically.

Ideally, this would involve plotting low vs. high on x3 on separate
plots;  low vs. high on x2 on separate (color) lines within each plot;
and low vs. high on x1 as left vs. right side of the x-axis.
Obviously, Y on y-axis for everything.

I imagine that some combination of interaction.plot() calls from base
R would work (although the help file seems to focus on two-way
interactions), but I would like to take advantage of the far superior
display of your package.

I know that facet_grid() can be used easily for the separate plots, I
am just struggling with the best way to code the other aspects of the
plot, which I know are not very complex.   Part of the issue is that
for this purpose I am NOT interested in plotting any raw data (nor the
full set of predicted values), just lines for each arbitrary set of
predictor values described above.  I'm not sure whether this would be
easiest by creating an intermediate summary-level dataset from the
regression coefficients, or whether it's something the summary
functions in ggplot() can do in one swoop.

As always, thanks in advance for any help or advice you can provide!

messages.subject: Re: line plot to visualize three-way lm interaction
messages.subject_clean: line plot to visualize three-way lm interaction
messages.body_plain:
Hi Keith,

The basic strategy for this type of problem is as follows.

# 1.  Create a grid of the response values you're interested in
grid <- expand.grid(
  # you do one variable with a finer resolution than the others
  # because this can go on the x axis
  x1 = seq(min(df$x1), max(df$x1), length = 20),
  # use quartiles for low, medium and high, or pick them yourself
  x2 = quantile(df$x2, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75),
  x3 = quantile(df$x3, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75)
)

# 2.  Compute predicted values
grid$y <- predict(mymodel, grid)

# 3. Plot
qplot(x1, y, data = grid, geom = "line") + facet_grid(x2 ~ x3)
qplot(x1, y, data = grid, geom = "line", colour = x2) + facet_grid(~ x3)

# You'll need to play around with where each of the three variables go
# to get the best view for your data/model.

# You should probably also repeat the same plots with the raw data
# just to check that you're not missing anything in the model.

Hadley

So I was about to reply to my own question (... once again. Sorry
everyone, I really need to look harder before resorting to ask the
list) when Hadley gave the solution I also found in the book:
	theme_set(theme_gray(base_size=9))

Yet, not respecting the pointsize of the device might still be
considered as a bug by some. Especially since there is a complex
interaction between base_size in ggplot and pointsize on the device.
As a rule of thumb, I found that pointsize and base_size must be equal
for ggplots to look harmonious (i.e. as in the book / as Hadley
supposedly designed them to be).

Example (to be run on OS X, but just replace quartz() by X11() on
linux and the result is the same)

library(ggplot2)

p = qplot(runif(5),runif(5)) + opts(title="A dumb plot")

# this is the default
theme_set(theme_grey(12))
quartz(width=5, height=4, pointsize=12)
p

# this has display issues (overwriting in legends etc.) because the
font size is too large compared to what the device "expects"
theme_set(theme_grey(25))
quartz(width=5, height=4, pointsize=8)
p

# when the pointsize is set accordingly, the proportions are
"harmonious" again (well, it still does not look great that's because
25 is much to big for this size of plot)
theme_set(theme_grey(25))
quartz(width=5, height=4, pointsize=25)
p

# Ahhh, that's better
theme_set(theme_grey(10))
quartz(width=5, height=4, pointsize=10)
p

Beyond this issue, I took this opportunity to try and fix some old
theming code I had. It is too bad that (for consistency and robustness
purposes I guess) the theming has had to become so complicated. Before
I could do:

foo <- list(grid.fill="white", grid.minour.colour="black")
.
.
.
ggtheme(foo)

an ggplot would modify *only* those two elements in the theme current
when ggtheme is called (which can be different fro; the one foo was
defined in) and keep the defaults for the rest. Now I must write:

theme_update(panel.background = theme_rect(fill = "white"),
panel.grid.minor = theme_line(colour = "black"))

which is significantly more convoluted but, more importantly does not
seem to be "storable" as easily. The only way I found to "store" the
modifications of a few theme properties was:

# store the current theme for reference
old = theme_get()
# go back to default
theme_set(theme_gray())
# do some modifs
theme_update(panel.background = theme_rect(fill = "white"),
panel.grid.minor = theme_line(colour = "black"))
# store the full theme: default + modifs in a variable
foo = theme_get()
# go back to state before doing all that
theme_set(old)
.
.
.
# somewhere else, use the modifications in foo
theme_set(foo)

Which kind of works, even though the appearance induced by foo now
depends on the environment in which theme_update was initially called
(i.e. the default gray here) not the one in which theme_set(foo) is
called later. But that might be for the best: it is more reliable/
predictable.
Yet it seems convoluted. Is there any easier way I missed?

JiHO

On 2009-May-13  , at 07:20 , squid wrote:

> I'm finding that the pdfs I write to (using code below) are gigantic
> and cause Word, Powerpoint, and Preview to struggle. For example, when
> I open a PDF using Preview, each layer of each figure is built slowly
> and painfully, taking more than 30 seconds even though the pdf might

The journal you are submitting to probably has some requirements in
terms of figure formats (such as EPS or TIFF 1200 dpi for line art,
TIFF 600 dpi for pictures, which are insane but classic ones). Given
your issues, you could indeed go the raster route, but R cannot
produce TIFF so just output PNG at the appropriate resolution and then
convert it to TIFF <rant>why, oh why are publishers still requiring
TIFF when PNG is a lossless compression and does not have the cross
platform issue TIFF has in the order of channels?</rant>
However, as others have mentioned, the issue might be with the type of
plot you are trying to produce rather than with the file format. I
would use geom_density2d with fill=..density.. instead of a scatter
plot with that many points.

JiHO

>
> Yes, that's exactly the problem - how do we add more dimensions to the coordinate system?  One approach would be to add a z position aesthetic, but that doesn't generalise terribly well for more than 3 dimensions.

But in ternary plots, there are only two independent variables; the
third one is 1-x-y.  The problem with the third (dependent) variable
is not how to map it to an aesthetic, but only how to associate a
scale with it to label it properly.

messages.subject: Questions about facet_grid()
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am trying to generate a faceted histogram, with a label indicating
the mean for each group. I am able to do this without setting margins
= T, as is the case in the upper part of the code. The lower part is
the same as the upper, except that I added the margins = T argument.

Questions:
1) It looks with margins = T argument, the labeling was messed up. Why
is this happening?

2) Is it possible to print out margins just for the columns with all
the labeling? What is the recommended way to put text on each graph?

Thanks,
Stanley

####################################

p <- ggplot(data = mpg, aes(cty)) +
	geom_histogram(fill = "steelblue") +
	facet_grid(class ~ cyl) +
	theme_grey(base_size = 8)

tbl <- cast(data = mpg, class ~ cyl, value = "cty", fun = function(x)
round(mean(x), 2) )
tbl.m <- melt(tbl, id = c("class", "cyl"))

p + geom_text(
	aes(x = 10, y = 12, label = value),
	data = tbl.m,
	size = 3
)

####################

p <- ggplot(data = mpg, aes(cty)) +
	geom_histogram(fill = "steelblue") +
	facet_grid(class ~ cyl, margins = T) +
	theme_grey(base_size = 8)

tbl <- cast(data = mpg, class ~ cyl, value = "cty", fun = function(x)
round(mean(x), 2), margins = T)
tbl.m <- melt(tbl, id = c("class", "cyl"))

p + geom_text(
	aes(x = 10, y = 12, label = value),
	data = tbl.m,
	size = 3
)

messages.subject: Re: Defining contour line levels for density2d
messages.subject_clean: Defining contour line levels for density2d
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stavros -

I think ideally what you want is something akin to scale_y_log10() or scale_colour_manual() for the contour lines, right?  Unfortunately, there's not a scale_contour.  Looking at the source, it doesn't appear that there's any way to specify where the lines are, either by enumeration or a function to determine them like log10.

I've played around with the code for a little and learned from Hadley's source how to make a contour plot setting the levels manually, but my fix isn't pretty.

library(MASS)

mu <- c(0,0)
(si <- matrix(c(3,2,2,2), 2, 2, byrow = T))
df <- data.frame(mvrnorm(1000, mu = mu, Sigma = si))

ggplot(aes(x = X1, y = X2), data = df) +
  geom_point()

ggplot(aes(x = X1, y = X2), data = df) +
  geom_density2d()

## manually calculate the lines where you want them

dens <- kde2d(df$X1, df$X2, n = 100)

cl <- contourLines(
  x = dens$x,
  y = dens$y,
  z = dens$z,
  levels = fullseq(range(dens$z), .01)
)

cl <- mapply(function(x, piece) {
  rbind(data.frame(x, piece = piece), c(NA, NA, NA))
  }, cl, seq_along(cl), SIMPLIFY = FALSE)
cl_df <- do.call('rbind', cl)

## make the plot with path

ggplot() +
  geom_path(aes(x = x, y = y, group = piece, colour = level),
    data = cl_df) +
  scale_colour_continuous(breaks = na.omit(unique(cl_df$level)))

As you can see, the levels are set by the levels = command within the contourLines command.  The sequence can, of course, be anything.

Perhaps there's an easier way to do it, but this will get it done in a pinch.

Cheers
david.

sorry for my first reply which overlooked the tiny problem that you
can't have two stats for one geom. So David is correct, you have to
compute the density outside of ggplot. However, once you do that,
there is no need to do all the rest manually too. You can use
geom_contour directly. See the second example in stat_density2d or :

library("ggplot2")
library("MASS")

d = data.frame(x=rnorm(1000),y=rnorm(1000))

dens = MASS::kde2d(d$x, d$y, n = 100)
densf = data.frame(expand.grid(x=dens$x, y=dens$y), z=as.vector(dens$z))

ggplot(densf, aes(x=x,y=y,z=z)) + geom_contour(breaks=seq(min(densf
$z), max(densf$z), length.out=10))
# this puts 10 equally spaced breaks but you could put whatever you
want in the breaks parameter

I hope this is more helpful.

JiHO

Hi all,

in the below example I have 2 distribution the mean of which I want to
write in the plot using geom_text.

I know I can create a dataframe indicating the positions where I want
the means to be plotted but is there a way to just indicate that I
want the text to be plotted let's say in the top-left corner without
specifying each position?

Sometimes what I do is just indicate one position and use jitter to
avoid overploting like in the example below but the problem is that
everything is misaligned. Thanks.

library("ggplot2")
library("plyr")
n=1000
df1<-data.frame(resp=rnorm(n,0,10),distribution="a")
df2<-data.frame(resp=rnorm(n,2,5),distribution="b")
df<-rbind(df1,df2)

compute.mean<-function(x) data.frame(mean=mean(x$resp))
means<-ddply(df,.(distribution),compute.mean)

p<-ggplot()
p<-p+ geom_freqpoly(data=df,aes
(x=resp,y=..density..,color=distribution),binwidth = 1)
p<-p+ geom_text(data=means,aes(x=-20,y=0.08,label=paste("mean:
",mean),color=distribution),
      legend=F,position=position_jitter(height=0.02))
p<-p+ xlim(-30,30)
p

ps: does someone know why the y-label shows '0.08' instead of
'density'?

On 2009-May-14  , at 00:45 , dani wrote:

library("ggplot2")
library("plyr")
n=1000
df1<-data.frame(resp=rnorm(n,0,10),distribution="a")
df2<-data.frame(resp=rnorm(n,2,5),distribution="b")
df<-rbind(df1,df2)

compute.mean<-function(x) data.frame(mean=mean(x$resp))
means<-ddply(df,.(distribution),compute.mean)

p <- ggplot()
p <- p +
geom_freqpoly
(data=df,aes(x=resp,y=..density..,color=distribution),binwidth = 1)

p <- p + xlim(-30,30)

# one solution:
p + annotate("text",x=-30,y=0.06,label=paste("mean:",means$mean,
collapse="\n"), hjust=0, vjust=0)
# NB: setting hjust and vjust this way sets the lower left corner of
the text to (x,y), which is easier to deal with that the default (text
centered)

> ps: does someone know why the y-label shows '0.08' instead of
> 'density'?

because you specified y=0.08 *inside* the aes call. So it maps the
variable "0,08" to y. Such scalar values need to be set as parameters,
not aesthetics = outside the aes call.

Now the remaining issue would be to map the color of the text to the
color of the curves. There are two solutions:
- using scale_colour_manual for the freqpoly and setting manually the
same colors in two annotate calls
- use a geom_text to draw the text but either this way:
         p + geom_text(data=means, mapping=aes(colour=distribution,
label=paste("mean:", mean)),x=-30,y=0.06, hjust=0, vjust=0)
i.e. with x and y outside the aes call, or by adding the coordinates
in two columns resp and density in the dataframe means, and mapping
those inside the aes call:
         means$resp=-30
         means$density=c(0.06, 0.07)
         p + geom_text(data=means, mapping=aes(x=resp, y=density,
colour=distribution, label=paste("mean:", mean)), hjust=0, vjust=0)

I hope that helps.

JiHO
---
