messages.subject: Plot order (what steps on what)
messages.body_plain:
If I'm not mistaken, ggplot plots geoms specified later in a plot spec
after, and on top of, geoms specified earlier.

Thus, + geom_line(...) + geom_point(...) plots the points on top of
the lines, and + geom_point(...) + geom_line(...) plots the lines on
top of the points. So I can control this by reordering the clauses.

How do I control the ordering within the geom?  It appears that
geom_point plots left-to-right, bottom-to-top, but what I would like
to do is to specify which values plot on top of which others.  The
typical case is that I have a scatterplot where I'm using color for
the third dimension, but in places where the dots are dense, I can't
see the rare case that I'm trying to pick out with color.  I suppose I
could divide the data into multiple classes, and do something like

     + geom_point( data = df[df$z<1,], ...) + geom_point (data =
df[df$z >= 1 | df$z < 2, ], ...) + ...

but that is obviously pretty messy.

Is there some way to control this with a z-variable?  What controls
the current ordering?  Is it in a modifiable position_ clause or
something?

Thanks,

               -s

In your example this is a pain, but most of the time this is really
helpful - you just make sure your variable names match and you don't
need to worry about redefining all the aesthetic mappings.  Think
about the ggplot call as setting the defaults that all of the other
layers inherit - you can make the defaults as comprehensive, or not,
as you like.

> The fact that plots, which have an inherently hierarchical structure, are
> squished into a linear sequence in the ggplot2 syntax, just hurts my head.
> Sometimes later layers affect earlier ones, and sometimes they don't.

Layers _never_ affect other layers.  Scales, coords and facetting all
override previous specifications.

> list for many of the plots I make, I'm going to have to abandon it, sad to

> into xmgrace, and manually set all of the little details that ggplot2 does
> so nicely. Hopefully the ongoing and very rapid improvements in the package
> and the documentation will help me through this.

You might want to switch to using ggplot() instead of qplot() -
sometimes it helps to be more explicit about what's going on.

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: 0.8.3 upgrade broke plot with stat_summary
messages.body_plain:
For the benefit of posterity, Hadley found a bug and fixed this problem. Thank you!

Another minor issue, though. When I use the smooth geom with grouping by color, the colors of the line in the legend looks desaturated. I think the alpha parameter that is supposed to just be affecting the ribbon is also affecting the line in the legend.

Demo:
m <- ggplot(movies, aes(x=round(rating), y=votes, color=mpaa))
m2 <- m + stat_summary(fun.data = "mean_cl_normal", geom = "smooth", size=2)
m2 + scale_y_log10()

At least on my screen (see attachment) I get faded-looking colors in the legend.

Now do:
m2 <- m + stat_summary(fun.data = "mean_cl_normal", geom = "smooth", size=2, alpha=.1)
m2 + scale_y_log10()

The grey overlaid ribbons look nicer, but the legend is even worse. I'd blame it on my error somehow in the second case, but the fact that it's a problem in the first case suggests a bug somewhere...

R 2.8.1, development version of ggplot2, Linux. The problem is present on the screen, and in both pdf and png exports via ggsave.

(Incidentally, there have been threads about this, but I have to add "dpi=72" to the ggsave command to get a good .png file...)

 -Harlan

messages.body_plain:
On 2009-May-15  , at 15:42 , Harlan Harris wrote:

> You might want to switch to using ggplot() instead of qplot() -
> sometimes it helps to be more explicit about what's going on.
>
> Yes, I'll do that.

 From the point of view of someone who learned ggplot, I would also
strongly advise to use the ggplot construct as much and as soon as
possible. qplot is nice to lure users into using ggplot, because the
syntax is close enough to that of other plotting systems. However, the
true nature and power of ggplot only became apparent once I used
ggplot().

I would even advise to use ggplot() as an empty container and build
the plot layer by layer, specifying almost everything in each geom. It
is more explicit what the variables in each layer are if you do
something like

	ggplot() + geom_point(data=foo, mapping=aes(x=x, y=y)) +
geom_path(data=bar, aes(x=x, y=y, colour=value))

Later down the road, you can recompress is in the form

	ggplot(aes(x=x,y=y)) + geom_point(data=foo) + geom_path(data=bar,
aes(colour=value))

where the aesthetics are shared by all later geoms. But I find that
most of the time there is little difference. Indeed, when I have two
sets of data with exactly the same names, it's usually that they are
on the exact same scale (same coordinates) so I can easily merge the
dataframes (with merge()) and use that in ggplot. Otherwise, the two
data frames are separated enough that each needs a complete geom
specifications anyway.

To sum, up, I would advise you to
- use constructs like
	ggplot(foo, aes(x=x,y=y, colour=bar)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth()
   when you have one simple data frame as input
- switch to full specification
	ggplot() + geom_point(data=foo, aes(x=x,y=y, colour=bar)) +
geom_path(data=bar, aes(x=lon, y=lat, size=value))
   as soon as your data source gets a little more complex.

I hope that helps and that you'll keep using ggplot.

JiHO

messages.body_plain:
JiHO, this is some really good advice, and thank you for taking the time to write it.
As with any complicated system, it's difficult for the authors of that system to fully understand what novices (such as myself) find difficult about that system. I'm trying to learn several things at once -- the "words" of ggplot2 (geom_line, scale_x_continuous, etc.) and the "grammar" of ggplot2. But the grammar has two properties that make it difficult to learn. First, it doesn't quite fit into the conceptual structures that I'm used to. It has the syntax (the +s and ()s) of a programming language, but if you think about it that way, the scoping rules make no sense whatsoever, with weird backwards dependencies and a total disregard for locality. It's internally defining a hierarchical representation of a plot, like what one might think of in a more traditional drawing or plotting system, but in a very sparse way, and there's currently no good way of seeing that representation to check whether the translation from the linear language to the hierarchical language is working. And second, there are a large number of ways of doing everything, so you can't easily "chunk" useful phrases and use them elsewhere (as adults do when learning a new spoken language). It's as if you were learning a new language, but half the people used a variant like Latin, where you can put anything in any order as long as you case-mark everything, and some people used a variant like Chinese, where there is a standard order for everything, and some people used a variant like Japanese, where everything is backward and written in three different alphabets. ggplot2's extremely flexible syntax may make it difficult to be widely adopted by the R community, without significant pedagogical changes. In particular, it may be possible to teach ggplot2 by defining a rigid subset of the syntax that allows you to do everything, but also allows people to apply their existing conceptual knowledge of how programming languages work. Combined with a better tool for visualizing the resulting hierarchical plot structure, ggplot2's remarkable elegance and power may become more accessible. I would urge Hadley and others working on "grammar for graphics" ideas to spend some time thinking about the incomplete cognitive representations that learners of the systems are using, and how those misconceptions can cause ongoing problems with learning. Perhaps the next major upgrade to the system could involve some thoughts along these lines.

I appreciate y'all's indulgence in my little rant... I really want to use ggplot2, but am frustrated by my own inability to fully figure it out.

 -Harlan

						angle=rep(pi/2, length(x)), ar = rep(1, length(x)),
						colour = "grey50", fill = "grey90", units.def="native") {

messages.subject: Re: puzzling facet_grid, data, and group interaction
messages.subject_clean: puzzling facet_grid, data, and group interaction
messages.body_plain:
Harlan,

If I may counter-rant: It doesn't matter if ggplot2 fits into any
conceptual structure that you're used to. If you want a tool that
does, use base graphics or lattice. It should definitely NOT change to
match your pre-existing concepts of how graphs work or what graphs
are. It has a different philosophy on purpose, and I think your main
problem comes from trying to force it into your programming-language
framework -- which does not really work -- and it causes a cascade of
misunderstanding.

My first question for you would be: why exactly are you using ggplot2?
Because it's easy to make a particular kind of graph with it? Because
the defaults look nicer to you? To be blunt, those are not reasons to
use ggplot2. I've recreated certain ggplot2 graphs in lattice, for
various reasons. Anything you can do in ggplot2, you can do it in
lattice, though not with the same philosophy. What ggplot2 offers is a
different philosophy, and that's what you seem to be objecting to.

Now don't get me wrong. I've had a similar conversation about 5 months
ago when I first picked up ggplot2. But more on that later... First,
some more questions. (Not being facetious or rhetorical here, I
actually would like to see answers.)

You keep mentioning that ggplot2 is hierarchical. In what way? Please
give some examples. I see it as refreshingly orthogonal, and that's a
huge boost over alternatives that blur concepts together. I really
can't think of anything that's hierarchical about ggplot2.

(I'll say I had problems when I first came to ggplot2 because of how
some of the orthogonal concepts are described and broken out. They
make sense overall, but as one example, "scale" means something very
different in ggplot2 than what you might think of coming from another
background. I've tried to think of perhaps a better way of describing
the concept than "scale", and offered various suggestions to Hadley of
how the documentation might step you through the concepts in finer
increments, to help dispel misunderstandings early. But think as I
may, it's hard to come up with a correct way to describe "scale" that
is accurate and yet avoids the misunderstandings that I had with
"scale".)

You keep mentioning its "programming language syntax" with "+'s and
()'s", but it has no syntax of its own, only the R's syntax, which ALL
alternatives must cope with. Parentheses are used for function calls,
as in every other package you will ever use in R. How is ggplot2
somehow different than anything else you do in R, parentheses-wise?

(Yes, it uses "+" where other graphics packages do not, but that is
because you can explicitly add to a graph object, which alternatives
really cannot do. (Base graphics, for example, has a half-baked system
where you are essentially drawing nearly-unrelated graphs to a window
without erasing between draws. This will paint you into a corner oft-
times, or cause you to jump through hoops to avoid issues that a
computer should handle for you.) It's certainly not that odd in light
of other kinds of data structures that can be combined in many
languages with "+", including things like "Hello" + " there!".)

You mention "locality" as if this were a programming language with
scope. What do you see the locality that it should be honoring and how
does it break down?

Having several ways to do something is a benefit, not a drawback. R
certainly provides several ways to approach any one task syntactically
-- if only something as basic as implicit versus explicit iteration --
and if you want to find the "right" or "best" package to accomplish a
particular task it gets crazy-confusing. Your analogy with different
human languages doesn't really do much for me. Are you objecting to
flexibility in general, or in the how Hadley's documentation teaches
ggplot2, or where?

In addition to my initial problems with concepts like "scale" (above),
there is a complication that I cannot put my finger on. I think there
are two issues arising from ggplot2 being very Lego-like: you have
many, many pieces that you can plug together. Which leads to:

1. It causes many subtle bugs to creep in. Which can result in
something you think SHOULD work not working and you get frustrated
with stupid ggplot2. It feels like ggplot2's just being opaque and non-
intuitive, but in fact it's a bug and what you're doing actually
should be working but it just feels like it's being weird and you're
left asking, "What's the 'ggplot2 way' of doing things that I'm not
getting?"

2. You can do some incredibly sophisticated graphs with just a few
characters in ggplot2, which can let you get deep into the woods
without realizing that you don't actually understand some basic
concepts. The alternative, however, is not very palatable: make it
work like other packages, where you have to do a lot of coding to get
what you want, so you have to understand everything along the way or
it simply doesn't happen.

3. The error messages are not always the best. I think Hadley's
admitted to that and is looking into what he can do about that.
(Unfortunately, it could be a pretty deep-seated problem that doesn't
admit to a good solution without a rewrite.)

The bottom line, for me, is that it seems that you're trying to push
ggplot2 into your pre-existing frameworks and "programming language"
is the closest framework for you and from that viewpoint, ggplot2
won't make much sense. But specific examples would help everyone
understand what your pointing out.

    Wayne

Hi,

I've just been bitten by what seems to be a very tricky bug. I want to
map both colour and size (area) to a variable, to make the differences
a bit more apparent, and *sometimes* throws an error.

It is data-dependent: it sometimes fails with a dummy dataset, it
always fails with mine.
The environment is also influent, which is very weird: the first test
with a dummy dataset works, then mine makes it fail, then retrying
with the same dummy dataset fails. Cleaning the namespace does not
help. Quitting R does not help either. In fact, I have to close the
terminal and open a new shell, start a new R session in it and then
the dummy example works again. Very very weird...

Anyway, here is some code:

library("ggplot2")

# Try with a dummy dataset
d = data.frame(x=1:10, y=runif(10), z=runif(10))
ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x,y, size=z, colour=z)) + scale_area()
# It works

# Get my data
system("curl http://dl.getdropbox.com/u/1047321/scores.csv >
scores.csv")
scores = read.csv("scores.csv")
ggplot(scores) + geom_point(aes(lon, lat, size=value, colour=value))
# OK
ggplot(scores) + geom_point(aes(lon, lat, size=value, colour=value)) +
scale_area()
# Error in data.frame(c("#404CB1FF", "#5E408BFF", "#7C3364FF",
"#9A263EFF" :
#  arguments imply differing number of rows: 4, 5

# Change names, just in case
scores = rename(scores, c(lat="y", lon="x", value="foo"))
ggplot(scores) + geom_point(aes(x, y, size=foo, colour=foo)) +
scale_area()
# Error in data.frame(c("#4849A7FF", "#5B418EFF", "#6F3975FF",
"#82315CFF",  :
#  arguments imply differing number of rows: 6, 4

# Retry with the orignal dummy dataset
ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x,y,size=z, colour=z)) + scale_area()
# Error in data.frame(c("#4D479FFF", "#683B7EFF", "#83305CFF",
"#9D253AFF" :
#  arguments imply differing number of rows: 4, 7

# Clean the environment and retry
rm(list=ls())

d = data.frame(x=1:10, y=runif(10), z=runif(10))
ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x,y,size=z, colour=z)) + scale_area()
# Still no luck

I hope someone can reproduce that and figure out what happens...

Thanks in advance.

JiHO

Someone helped me figure out off list that the reproducibility of my
example actually depends on the random seed. So the bug is indeed data
dependent but you don't have to download my data to see it.

As for:

> The environment is also influent, which is very weird: the first
> test with a dummy dataset works, then mine makes it fail, then
> retrying with the same dummy dataset fails. Cleaning the namespace
> does not help. Quitting R does not help either. In fact, I have to
> close the terminal and open a new shell, start a new R session in it
> and then the dummy example works again. Very very weird...

this seems to be completely wrong. Indeed, today, when the plot works
with a given dataset, it always does, no matter what happens in
between. I don't know what I drank last night which made me think
otherwise...

So now I can give a minimal reproducible example:

library("ggplot2")

set.seed(1)

d = data.frame(x=1:10, y=runif(10), z=runif(10))
ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x,y, size=z, colour=z)) + scale_area()

# fails

set.seed(7)

d = data.frame(x=1:10, y=runif(10), z=runif(10))
ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x,y, size=z, colour=z)) + scale_area()

# works

1 to 6 fail, 7, 8, 9 work, 10 fails etc.

Thank you very much to Mike Lawrence for helping me. I hope it will
help figure out the bug.

On Sat, May 16, 2009 at 10:29 PM, Wayne Folta <wd...@mac.com> wrote:
> If I may counter-rant: It doesn't matter if ggplot2 fits into any
> conceptual structure that you're used to. If you want a tool that
> does, use base graphics or lattice. It should definitely NOT change to
> match your pre-existing concepts of how graphs work or what graphs
> are.

Speaking for myself (though I suspect that Harlan would agree), I very much like ggplot's conceptual structure of graphs.  It makes much more sense to me than base graphics or lattice graphics.  That is not the issue at all.

What I have had more trouble with is the notation for that conceptual structure.  I find it hard to put my finger on what exactly the problem is, but the use of '+' (normally a commutative, associative operator) to express a rather complicated hierarchical relationship might be part of it. Another part of it is the handy (but again complicated) defaults.

I find Mike Lawrence's suggestion to use only 'layer' intriguing and might try it.  Maybe that will make things simpler for me. Having three different notations defined for ggplot (qplot, geom_xxx, and layer) is confusing.  I guess Hadley assumed that readers of his book will be coming from R base graphics, but if I were teaching R + plotting, I would want to skip base graphics entirely....

> It has a different philosophy on purpose, and I think your main problem comes from trying to force it into your programming-language framework -- which does not really work -- and it causes a cascade of misunderstanding.

Not sure what you mean here.  ggplot *is* a programming language, and it is also embedded into a programming language.  To the extent that ggplot's semantics are inconsistent with those of the embedding language, there is bound to be confusion.

> ...You keep mentioning that ggplot2 is hierarchical. In what way? Please
> give some examples.

I don't know if this is what Harlan had in mind, but for me, the very simplest example is things like:

    ggplot(data=qq) +
        geom_point(aes(x=a,y=b)) +
        geom_point(aes(x=c,y=d)) +
        coordxxx()

which really means something like

     with( list(data=qq),
               coordxxx(     # coord applies to the whole stack of layers
                  stack_layers( geom_point( aes(x=a,y=b) ),   # a and b are w.r.t. qq
                                         geom_point(aes(x=c,y=d)) ) ) )

(note the nesting)

By the way, a strange (but not necessarily very practical) case I constructed:

     test <- data.frame(a=1:4,b=4:1)
     ggplot() + local({
             qq <- test
             geom_point(data=qq,aes(x=a,y=b) )
            } ) # works fine

     test <- data.frame(x=1:4,y=4:1)
     ggplot() + local({
             qq <- test
             k <- 3
             geom_point(data=qq,aes(x=x,y=y^k) )
            } )
# error: object "k" not found

> 1. ...something you think SHOULD work not working and you get frustrated

>
> with stupid ggplot2. It feels like ggplot2's just being opaque and non-
> intuitive, but in fact it's a bug and what you're doing actually
> should be working but it just feels like it's being weird and you're
> left asking, "What's the 'ggplot2 way' of doing things that I'm not
> getting?"

Yes, I have run into this too.

> 3. The error messages are not always the best. I think Hadley's
> admitted to that and is looking into what he can do about that.

Yes, I have raised this issue, too.

               -s

On 2009-May-16  , at 22:29 , Wayne Folta wrote:

> The bottom line, for me, is that it seems that you're trying to push
> ggplot2 into your pre-existing frameworks and "programming language"
> is the closest framework for you and from that viewpoint, ggplot2
> won't make much sense.

I would like to second that. My impression after reading your first
question and "rant" is that your problem comes from knowing too much
already. Your preconceived ideas are impairing your learning of
ggplot. To re-use your metaphor: have you ever noticed how hard it is
to learn a new language for grown-ups, while kids/teenagers pick that
in a blast?. So, even though this is just commonplace talk, I think
you should try to forget a bit what you know and come to ggplot with a
fresher mind.

Not having much experience in base R graphics or extended knowledge or
programming languages structure, I found ggplot very intuitive: you're
just building the plot layer by layer, linking the properties of your
data to graphical representations. Sure there are some edge cases and
some less intuitive stuff (the scales in particular can be tricky).
But overall, the fact that ggplot rests upon a real "system" (the
grammar or graphics) makes it clearer than other plotting systems.

Finally, regarding the implementation, I agree that having several
ways of doing the same thing is confusing. I tend to prefer simple,
reliable "things" over fancy, hyper-configurable ones. As other
posters, I think that having ggplot() + layer() + scale() would have
been sufficient, even though the syntax is longer (but I started with
ggplot + geom so now I stick to that). However, I  also understand the
necessity of providing qplot or other simplified, more usual,
interfaces.
The thing is, each of us does not *have* to use all the complexity.
You can choose to use only a subset of the language and stick to it,
to ease up the learning. I recommended ggplot() + geom_* earlier.
That's probably the most documented. But if you want a very strong and
conservative structure, ggplot + layer is probably better.

JiHO

Stavros,

> I don't know if this is what Harlan had in mind, but for me, the
> very simplest example is things like:
>
>     ggplot(data=qq) +
>         geom_point(aes(x=a,y=b)) +
>         geom_point(aes(x=c,y=d)) +
>         coordxxx()
>
> which really means something like
>
>      with( list(data=qq),
>                coordxxx(     # coord applies to the whole stack of
> layers
>                   stack_layers( geom_point( aes(x=a,y=b) ),   # a
> and b are w.r.t. qq
>
> geom_point(aes(x=c,y=d)) ) ) )
>

Good example!

I've rewritten this reply multiple times, and finally think I see the
core issue here: your "really means" rephrasing of the ggplot2 code is
execution-oriented. It is the way that ggplot2 would work if it had
the same philosophy as base graphics: when geom_point() is called, it
would literally draw stuff on the page.

But rather, ggplot2 is about creating an object and setting
properties, then causing it to plot by printing it. It's object-
oriented, and the ggplot(data=qq) is creating an object with several
default properties and one explicit property. The coordxxx() is
setting some more properties of this object. The geom_point()'s are
setting properties, which themselves are objects which inherit some
properties from the ggplot2 object and have some properties of their
own.

So there is a hierarchy, but it's an OO kind of hierarchy. It takes
the human phrasing of a graph: "Create a graph using data from the
dataframe qq. The first layer is an x-y plot using dots to plot a
versus b. The second layer is an x-y plot using dots to plot c versus
d. The graph's coordinate system is xxx." But maps it into something
like:

    gg = new (ggplot)
    gg.data = qq

    gg.layer[1].style = points
    gg.layer[1].data = (:a, :b)

    gg.layer[2].style = points
    gg.layer[2].data = (:c, :d)

    gg.coords = "xxx"

    gg.plot ()

(where I've made up the ":a" to indicate that a is chosen from the
object's default data.) There is an obvious class hierarchy here, but
the statements are not nested, just as in ggplot2. And in fact, you
can rearrange those statements rather arbitrarily, setting gg.coords
before the layers or after the layers, etc, just as in ggplot2.

Does that make sense?

    Wayne

> ...I've rewritten this reply multiple times, and finally think I see the

> core issue here: your "really means" rephrasing of the ggplot2 code is

Not at all!  It is organized in terms of the logical relationships
among the parts: where do the geoms look to find the data they refer
to (they look in the parent ggplot)? What plots are affected by coords
or scales (all of them)?  etc.

> ...So there is a hierarchy, but it's an OO kind of hierarchy....

Not really.

> "Create a graph using data from the
> dataframe qq. The first layer is an x-y plot using dots to plot a
> versus b. The second layer is an x-y plot using dots to plot c versus
> d. The graph's coordinate system is xxx."

OK, I'll take that as a paraphrase. Note the interesting use of "the
graph's" coordinate system as opposed to "its" coordinate system.
That expresses the structure of the relationship of the coordinate
system to the graph as a whole (as opposed to one of the layers).
That is the kind of structure I am talking about.

> But maps it into something like:
>
>    gg = new (ggplot)
>    gg.data = qq
>
>    gg.layer[1].style = points
>    gg.layer[1].data = (:a, :b)
>
>    gg.layer[2].style = points
>    gg.layer[2].data = (:c, :d)
>
>    gg.coords = "xxx"
>
>    gg.plot ()
>
> (where I've made up the ":a" to indicate that a is chosen from the
> object's default data.) There is an obvious class hierarchy here, but
> the statements are not nested, just as in ggplot2. And in fact, you
> can rearrange those statements rather arbitrarily, setting gg.coords
> before the layers or after the layers, etc, just as in ggplot2.
>
> Does that make sense?

Both of your paraphrases are explicit about the hierarchical
relations.  They are implicit in ggplot.  I am not sure whether that
is good or bad, but it is definitely something you have to learn....

         -s

Stavros, I completely agree. Thank you for clarifying my ideas so
well, and yes, the example gets exactly at my notion of hierarchiy. I
love the idea behind building up graphs in ggplot, and the way the
data, and the facets, and the aesthetic elements "just work" together
(usually). The difficulty I have is working backwards, from the plot
that I've designed on paper, back to the syntax that generates that
plot.

Wayne, I think that your statement that it doesn't matter if people
can use their existing concepts to learn it is a very user-unfriendly
way to think about this tool. Are you a UNIX hacker, by chance? :) The
grammar for graphics philosophy, as I understand it, is partly to make
it easy to create graphs that elegantly tell the story of data. If
people are scared off from using it, because the analogies that
they're drawing are false analogies, then they won't use this tool.
Heck, they'll probably use Excel instead, and that'll be the end of
civilization!

> I find Mike Lawrence's suggestion to use only 'layer' intriguing and might
> try it.  Maybe that will make things simpler for me.

Yes, me too. I've never used layer explicitly, and perhaps that will
help me build up the conceptual structures to really grok ggplot's
details. (I'll report back on this experiment!)

> Having three different
> notations defined for ggplot (qplot, geom_xxx, and layer) is confusing.  I
> guess Hadley assumed that readers of his book will be coming from R base
> graphics, but if I were teaching R + plotting, I would want to skip base
> graphics entirely....

Yes, I learned R by reading Muenchen's "R for SAS and SPSS Users"
book, which is quite glowing about ggplot2. But I had no knowledge of
base graphics or anything else before starting to use ggplot. The only
command-line plotting tool I'd used recently is matlab, which is very
procedural and traditional (and limited).

JoHO says:
>I would like to second that. My impression after reading your first
>question and "rant" is that your problem comes from knowing too much
>already. Your preconceived ideas are impairing your learning of
>ggplot. To re-use your metaphor: have you ever noticed how hard it is
>to learn a new language for grown-ups, while kids/teenagers pick that
>in a blast?. So, even though this is just commonplace talk, I think
>you should try to forget a bit what you know and come to ggplot with a
>fresher mind.

Easier said than done! I actually study the role of prior knowledge in
conceptual learning. It's pretty hard to turn off relying on concepts
that you know when you're learning something new. People are
analogical creatures, and trying to wish it away doesn't work very
well.

Like I've said before, I really like the idea of building up a "plan"
for a graph, independent of the data, then applying the data to it.
And I really like the way ggplot fills in the blanks in your
specification in such an elegant way. But I'm not totally convinced
that the linear construction of the specification is conceptually
clearest. I realize it violates a lot of the basics of R and ggplot,
but you (read "I") almost want a GUI to put the pieces together.
Something a little like Simulink in Matlab, maybe. You wouldn't
manipulate the *data*, like in Excel, but instead you manipulate the
pieces of the data structure that define the plot. A box for a layer,
with sub-boxes for a layer's components. Shared components get linked
together (visually). Aesthetics map from the data frame to parameters
of a geom object. This tool could show what the equivalent code would
be (for educational purposes if nothing else), and could generate the
R object that you could use to make a plot. Hadley, you need an
intern!

Thanks everyone for the comments and suggestions,

 -Harlan

I'm not advocating make it complicated for complexity's sake. Rather,
I am looking at ggplot2 compared to every other alternative that I'm
aware of -- especially in R -- and I love it for the difference, for
its philosophy. You seem to be arguing that it should in fact be more
like everything else, or at least the parts of "everything else" that
you've become familiar and comfortable with.

It's like you want to learn Lisp because of all the cool things it can
do, except you hate those parentheses, and you hate prefix notation,
and you'd rather have functions named similarly to C, and..., and at
some point you've created C again, perhaps with a "taste of Lisp" in
there somewhere. (Or you want to learn Spanish, but can't roll your
R's, and don't like the word ordering, and don't like the concept of
gender, and... soon you have English.)

So yes, as someone who has adopted ggplot2 because of the way it is
different from everything else, I say "it's got a long learning curve,
but it's worth it". Please don't turn ggplot2 into lattice with a
couple of fancier graph types.

> Something a little like Simulink in Matlab, maybe. You wouldn't
> manipulate the *data*, like in Excel, but instead you manipulate the

A nice vision, and perhaps I misunderstood you, above! At the same
time, I've seen graphical programming environments that look pretty,
but actually take a LOT more work (and are more confusing)  than
something more linear. Why can't I hook up a wire from this port to
that port? Why does this box seem to work synchronously, while that is
asynchronously, and what kind of buffer do I need between them? I want
to reuse something I did, and doing a copy/paste, then going into all
of the dialog boxes to fix things is slower than tediously rewiring a
new setup. Etc...

(Not to mention that R doesn't even have useful, standardized,
interactive graphical environments yet, much less the ggplot5 you're
talking about. ;-))

I think the data=qq part is different from the rest of the argument to
the extent that it is a scoping-like rule that is radically different
from every language out there, including basic R. So it is confusing
in one sense, and perhaps could be eliminated from ggplot2 without
major trauma to the overall philosophy. At the same time, every
formula-using function I can think of in R has a data= which works the
same way, so it's not like Hadley made this up out of nowhere. (And in
fact, there are several advantages with doing it this way, confusing
though it may be initially.)

Leaving data= aside, I still hearing you talking in low-level,
executable terms. "Where do geoms look", "what plots are affected by",
etc, and I think that this is technically correct, but not the way to
think of ggplot2. Just as you can take "mean (a$x)" at face value, or
you can begin to get into: mean depends on a$x, which depends on a,
which is implemented as a linked list of linked lists, and mean() may
be a generic function, which depends on the class of x, and ..., and
soon you're lost in the weeds of compiler design. If you want it to
be, "mean (a$x)" is deeply hierarchical in a number of ways, both
explicit and implicit, and if you allow yourself to look at it as if
you were a C programmer implementing R it will be confusing rather
than illuminating.

A ggplot2 object contains a data frame from which it draws the data it
plots (data=). It has a coordinate system type to map from data space
to display space (coord). It has attributes describing one or more
subsets of data that should be displayed (aes, etc). Each subset of
the data (subset in terms of both columns and rows of data) can be
preprocessed mathematically, replacing or augmenting the data (stat).
Each subset can have a different presentation of the (possibly
preprocessed) points in aggregate (geom) and also individually
(scale). Etc.

Is a stat below or above a geom, or neither? Is a scale above or below
a coord, or neither? Is choosing columns of data to display (aes)
above or below choosing rows, or neither? Is a geom below a coord? You
seem to imagine that the geom "draws", looking to the coord to
determine how to draw. But it could as likely be that the geom "draws"
and its pixels are warped by the coord. Both of those are
implementation details: the meaningful distinction is that a ggplot
object displays using a coord and overlaying multiple geoms.

So, going back to the original rant, is ggplot2 hiding all kinds of
meaningful hierarchy with weird syntax? Is it making you guess things
that are implicit that should be explicit? I say no, with the arguable
exception of data=.

There's a long learning curve to ggplot2, but I think it's mostly
because of what we've used before, that has trained us to think in a
certain way about graphs, and that has trained us to expect its
functionality to fall along the grain instead of across.

messages.subject: Re: [R] Coord_equal in ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
(following up on the ggplot2 mailing list)

There seem to be some bugs in coord_equal -- or perhaps in the documentation.  The documentation in effect makes it sound on the one hand as though the ratio specifies the ratio of the x/y scales and then in the next sentence make it sound as though it specifies the ratio of the x/y plotting dimensions:

     ...one parameter, 'ratio', which specifies
     the ratio between the x and y scales. An aspect ratio of two means
     that the plot will be twice as high as wide.  An aspection [sic] ratio
     of 1/2 means that the plot will be twice as wide as high.  By
     default, the aspect.ratio of the plot will also be set to this value.

The last sentence makes it sound as though the 'ratio' is distinct from the 'aspect.ratio', but the preceding sentence calls the 'ratio' the 'aspect ratio'.  All very confusing.

But as I understand the overall intent, coord_equal() is defined to give equal *scales* on the two axes.  As a side-effect, it also sets aspect.ratio to 1 (why?). (aspect.ratio is an undocumented parameter to opts which apparently means the aspect ratio of the plot area and presumably does not change the scales).

pp <- ggplot(data=data.frame(a=1:4,b=2^(1:4))) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=b))

This gives (correctly, I think) a square plot with x = -4..10 and y=2..16:
     pp + coord_equal()

This gives (incorrectly, I think) a tall, narrow plot, and doesn't limit x to 0..5:
     pp + coord_equal() + xlim(0,5)

This gives (correctly, I think) a square plot with equal scales:
     pp + coord_equal() + ylim(0,100)

This gives (incorrectly, I think) a tall, narrow plot with unequal scales:
     pp + coord_equal() + opts(aspect.ratio = 10)

This gives (incorrectly, I think) a square plot with equal scales (apparently coord_equal's *default* setting of aspect.ratio is overriding the *explicit* setting of aspect.ratio, which seems wrong):
    pp + opts(aspect.ratio = 10) + coord_equal()

Help!

              -s

messages.subject: RE: [R] Coord_equal in ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
Hi Hadley,

Here are some examples and what I would expect them to do. I would suggest to split the ratio parameter into scale and aspect.

library(ggplot2)
ds <- data.frame(

	x = runif(1000, min = 0, max = 300000),
	y = runif(1000, min = 140000, max = 260000))

ggplot(ds, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point() + coord_equal()

# a square plot with the same scale on both axis.

ggplot(ds, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point() + coord_equal() + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 300000)) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(140000, 260000))

# a non square plot with the same scale on both axis

ggplot(ds, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point() + coord_equal(scale = 2/5, aspect = 1)
# a square plot. 2 cm on the X-axis equals 5 cm on the Y-axis

ggplot(ds, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point() + coord_equal(scale = 1, aspect = 2/5)
# a plot that is 2/5 times higher than wide. The scale on both axes is the same.

Best regards,

Thierry

Onderwerp: Re: [R] Coord_equal in ggplot2

On Tue, May 19, 2009 at 11:44 AM, Stavros Macrakis <macr...@gmail.com> wrote:

> (following up on the ggplot2 mailing list)
>
> There seem to be some bugs in coord_equal -- or perhaps in the
> documentation.  The documentation in effect makes it sound on the one
> hand as though the ratio specifies the ratio of the x/y scales and
> then in the next sentence make it sound as though it specifies the
> ratio of the x/y plotting dimensions:

It does both.  The aspect ratio needs to match the "scale" ratio, otherwise you can resize the plot so that the scale ratio doesn't match.

>      ...one parameter, 'ratio', which specifies
>      the ratio between the x and y scales. An aspect ratio of two
> means
>      that the plot will be twice as high as wide.  An aspection [sic]
> ratio
>      of 1/2 means that the plot will be twice as wide as high.  By
>      default, the aspect.ratio of the plot will also be set to this value.
>
> The last sentence makes it sound as though the 'ratio' is distinct
> from the 'aspect.ratio', but the preceding sentence calls the 'ratio'
> the 'aspect ratio'.  All very confusing.
>
> But as I understand the overall intent, coord_equal() is defined to
> give equal *scales* on the two axes.  As a side-effect, it also sets
> aspect.ratio to 1 (why?). (aspect.ratio is an undocumented parameter
> to opts which apparently means the aspect ratio of the plot area and
> presumably does not change the scales).

Correct.  See above for why.

> pp <- ggplot(data=data.frame(a=1:4,b=2^(1:4))) +
> geom_point(aes(x=a,y=b))
>
> This gives (correctly, I think) a square plot with x = -4..10 and y=2..16:
>      pp + coord_equal()
>
> This gives (incorrectly, I think) a tall, narrow plot, and doesn't
> limit x to 0..5:
>      pp + coord_equal() + xlim(0,5)
>
> This gives (correctly, I think) a square plot with equal scales:
>      pp + coord_equal() + ylim(0,100)
>
> This gives (incorrectly, I think) a tall, narrow plot with unequal scales:
>      pp + coord_equal() + opts(aspect.ratio = 10)
>
> This gives (incorrectly, I think) a square plot with equal scales
> (apparently coord_equal's *default* setting of aspect.ratio is
> overriding the *explicit* setting of aspect.ratio, which seems wrong):
>     pp + opts(aspect.ratio = 10) + coord_equal()

If anyone could give me a comprehensive set of test cases (with all combinations of setting x, y and ratio) and what they expect I could come up with an algorithm, but the behaviour is currently poorly defined because I don't really understand what people want/expect.

Hadley

messages.subject: ggplot correlation matrix
messages.body_plain:
Hi gang,

I'm playing with a ggplot2 based correlation matrix, mostly insipred
by this non-ggplot example:
http://addictedtor.free.fr/graphiques/graphcode.php?graph=137

My version is attached, and I'm pretty happy with it. Panels below the
diagonal contain the data and lm fits, panels above the diagonal
contain a text representation of the correlation estimate, colored
reddish if the correlation p-value is less than .05, blueish if the
correlation p-value is greater than .05, and sized proportional to
r^2.

There's only a few tweaks I'd like to make:

(1) Get rid of the standard facet labels, which are redundant to the
diagonal labels

(2) Let the scales vary freely for each panel. Right now I convert the
measures to z-scores, so at least they're on scales that generally fit
together, but if there are large outliers in one panel it would be
nice for that not to affect the scales of the other panels. setting
"scales='free'" in the facet_grid call simply lets each row to vary &
each column to vary, but with a row, y-scale is fixed and within a
column x-axis is fixed.

It might be nice to somehow make var_text_size & cor_text_limits
automatic, but I doubt this is feasible.

I also had a thought: Maybe it would be more useful to plot the
residuals instead of the raw data?

Any input would be greatly appreciated!

Mike

--

Department of Psychology
Dalhousie University

messages.subject: Suggestion for improvement: thoughts about scale_size
messages.subject_clean: Suggestion for improvement: thoughts about scale_size
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

Currently scale_size provides scales that are absolute: not relative
to the size of the viewport or the x/y scales of the plot. Therefore,
rescaling the plotting device changes the aspect of the plot.

Example:

x = y = 1:10
d = expand.grid(x=x,y=y)
set.seed(1)
d$value = runif(100)
p = qplot(x,y,size=value, data=d) + scale_size(to=c(0,15))
pdf("foo1.pdf", width=6,height=6)
     print(p)
dev.off()
pdf("foo2.pdf", width=4,height=4)
     print(p)
dev.off()
system("open foo1.pdf foo2.pdf")
# In the second case, the dots are much to big and overlap.

This means that once the plot looks good on screen, there is still a
lot of trial and error left to have it look OK on print, because the
size is likely to be different. And this has to be repeated for each
new size the plot has to take.
It would be more useful to have a measure of scale that would be:
	- either in the same unit as the coordinates of the plot, which would
make selecting the correct size much easier
	- or, if the above is not possible, at least proportional to the size
of the device, so that rescaling the device also rescales the dots,
instead of just replotting them at the same size.

What do other users think about that? Do you see an advantage to the
current behaviour? How difficult would it be to change that Hadley?

Thanks in advance for your opinion. Sincerely,

JiHO
---

messages.subject: Colorblind-friendly palette?
messages.body_plain:
I just came across a page on making presentations that don't cause problems for those that are colorblind:
http://jfly.iam.u-tokyo.ac.jp/color/

On that page, there is a set of colors that is both aesthetically pleasing  and colorblind-friendly. Hadley - how do you feel about adding a color scale like this? I think it would be beneficial -- perhaps even as the default color set -- since something like 8% of men have some form of colorblindness. I recently showed a colorblind friend a graph generated with ggplot2, and he had a bit of difficulty distinguishing the reds and greens (he could see that there was a difference, but the difference wasn't obvious).

I'm looking at the code for scale-discrete-colour.r and I might try playing it, but I can't say that I fully understand how it works just yet.

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: remove the legend but keeping the space
messages.subject_clean: remove the legend but keeping the space
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I can think of two situations but it's hard to tell without reproducible code,

1) the page layout is a result of facetting (possibly with a dummy
factor) or wrapping, in which case there should be one common legend
and its default position should be nicely aligned in the page

2) you don't want to use the first option, so you've placed two
unrelated ggplots on a page using grid.layout or other viewport
functions. Perhaps you can do something like this,

- create your two plots p1 and p2

- save the legend of p1 as a grob,

p3 <- p1 + opts(keep= "legend_box")

- strip the legend of p1 and p2,

p1 <- p1 + opts(legend.position = "none")
p2 <- p2 + opts(legend.position = "none")

- create three viewports on the page and print p1, p2, p3.

Example:

The main problem is that grid doesn't have any drawing primitives that
allow you to specify size in native units.  The only way I can see to
get it to work would be to use polygons to reproduce (e.g.) points and
lines.  This would be a lot slower than the usual drawing, and I think
would be most appropriate as new geoms.  I suspect points and lines
would cover 95% of all use cases.

Hadley

messages.subject: Quantile-quantile plot
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to create a quantile-quantile plot of two sample distributions.  This is not the same as stat_qq, which is a sample/theoretical plot (apparently the standard name for that is not a quantile-quantile plot, but a "probability plot" -- http://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/probplot.htm).

I can do this for a single case very simply:

# Distributions to compare
dist1 <- c(rnorm(100,1,1),rnorm(100,3,1))
dist2 <- c(rnorm(50,2,1),rnorm(300,3,1))

# Calculated quantiles
q1 <- quantile(dist1,0:100/100)
q2 <- quantile(dist2,0:100/100)

ggplot(data=data.frame(a=q1,b=q2)) +
   geom_line(aes(x=a,y=b)) +
   geom_abline(intercept=0,slope=1)

This works fine.

However, I can't figure out how to do the usual beautiful ggplot slice-and-dice (colors, facets) with different subsets of the distributions.

One thought I had was to define a scale -- perhaps this is the intent of the undocumented scale_xx_prob? But even if I could do that, I don't see how I'd get the data in, since ggplot requires observations to come in as a single data frame where x's and y's are linked.  In the case of comparing distributions, the count may be different both for the full data set and for subsets, and the data points aren't linked.

Ideas?

            -s

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

JiHo's asked me about a possible modification to the segments geom.
Instead of mapping x, y, xend, yend, one could provide a set of x,y,
angle, length.

One option is to create a new geom, but since the end result is
identical to geom_segment this seems redundant. Another option I
envisaged is to provide additional parameters to geom_segment, but I'm
not sure it can work.

Here's an illustration,

fieldGrob <- function(x, y,
	xend=x+length*cos(angle), yend=y+length*sin(angle),
	angle=atan((yend - y)/(xend - x)), length=sqrt((x-xend)^2 + (y-yend)^2),
	colour="black", fill=colour, size=1, linetype=1, arrow=NULL) {

		segmentsGrob(x, y, xend, yend, default.units="native",
	            gp = gpar(col=colour, fill=colour,
lwd=size*ggplot2:::.pt, lty=linetype, lineend = "butt"),
	            arrow = arrow)
}

fieldGrob(0.5, 0.5, 0.6, 0.6)->g1
fieldGrob(0.5, 0.5, , , pi/6, 0.2, col="blue")->g2
pushViewport(vp=viewport(width=1, height=1))
grid.draw(g1)
grid.draw(g2)

This grob could replace segmentsGrob in the code for geom_segment, but
my attempt at doing so failed (something still expected xend and yend)
and I'm not completely sure it can work.

Another solution is to transform the original data, as in,

field2segment <- function(d=NULL, ...){
	transform(d,
		x=x - 0.5*length*cos(angle), y=y - 0.5*length*sin(angle),
		# x and y shifted from the middle to the extremity of the segment
		xend=x+0.5*length*cos(angle), yend=y+0.5*length*sin(angle) )
}

xy <- expand.grid(x=-10:10, y=-10:10)
d1 <- data.frame(x=xy$x, y=xy$y)
d1$colour <- sample(1:5, length(xy$x), repl=T) # check that other
aesth. are handled well

d1$angle <- 2*pi*rnorm(d1$x)
d1$length <- rnorm(d1$y)

d2 <- field2segment(d1)

p <- ggplot(map=aes(x=x, y=y, colour=colour))

p + geom_segment(data=d1, map=aes(xend=xend, yend=yend)) # fails as
xend and yend are missing
p + geom_segment(data=d2, map=aes(xend=xend, yend=yend)) # works

If I understand correctly JiHo's request (correct me if I missed the
point altogether!), what we're after is perhaps a more convenient
interface for this operation. Any suggestions?

baptiste

PS: by the by, a very similar question arose recently with the
parametrisation of ellipses: I chose x, y, angle, aspect ratio (a/b),
whilst other packages (e.g. ellipse) seem the prefer a
covariance-correlation matrix. Assuming we figure the best way to deal
with such a dual parametrisation as discussed above, does anyone know
the correspondence between the two formulations?

messages.subject: mapping variables by transparency ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
is there a way to map a variable by degree of transparency/lightness
of the color? In the following example, I want to map var2 by
intensity, not by shape:

library("ggplot2")
df1<-data.frame(x=c(1,2),y=c(1,1),var1="a",var2=T)
df2<-data.frame(x=c(1,2),y=c(2,2),var1="b",var2=T)
df3<-data.frame(x=c(4,5),y=c(7,8),var1="b",var2=F)
df<-rbind(df1,df2,df3)

p<-ggplot(data=df,aes(x=x,y=y,color=var1,shape=var2))
p<-p+geom_point()
p

but something like

p<-ggplot(data=df,aes(x=x,y=y,color=var1,alpha=var2))

does not work (Error: Continuous variable (var2) supplied to discrete
scale_shape)

Thanks.

--
Daniel Linares

messages.subject: facet + free scales + coord flip
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Free scales in facetting do not seem to take coord_clip into account:

set.seed(1)
d = data.frame(variable=rep(c("foo","bar"), each=10), x = 1:10, value
= c(runif(10, 1, 10), runif(10, 100, 200)))

ggplot(d, aes(x=x)) + geom_path(aes(y=value)) + coord_flip() +
facet_grid(.~variable, scales="free")
# even though, due to coord flip, the y scale is at the bottom and can
be free, it is not

# I cannot switch x and y since my ultimate goal involves geom_ribbon
ggplot(d, aes(x=x)) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=value-3, ymax=value+3)) +
coord_flip() + facet_grid(.~variable, scales="free")
# and geom ribbon only takes ymin and ymax arguments (not xmin and xmax)

# So the solution is to do the facetting in the other dimension
ggplot(d, aes(x=x)) + geom_path(aes(y=value)) + facet_grid(variable~.,
scales="free")
# But the result is not really what I want (my x scale is a depth and
it would of course be nicer to have it vertical)

I'll experiment with geom polygon to try and create the ribbon
manually. That's the only solution I can see right now.
Thanks in advance for any pointer/other workarounds.

JiHO
---

library(MASS)

  layer(geom="point") +
  layer(geom="smooth", method="rlm") +
  labs(x=NULL, y="Communist vote share (per cent)")

where the post1991 factor is being used to split the data into two
groups, and rlm() is being used on them separately.

-----------------------
ggplot(tmp, aes(dates, vshare)) +
  layer(geom="point", colour=factor(post1991)) +

  labs(x=NULL, y="Communist vote share (per cent)")
------------------------

which is a single rlm() over the entire dataset, and the post1991
factor only matters in changing the colour scheme.

I am not able to understand why this tiny change is doing so much.
Could you please explain?

On 2009-May-22  , at 05:32 , baptiste auguie wrote:

> Well, with some help from the morning coffee I realise I was being
> dumb as there's a big problem with the last idea I proposed: there is
> no way to map the angle and length to variables of the original
> data.frame and have them appear in the legend.

The transformation you propose in your second solution is what I am
doing currently. However, the goal is indeed to have the length and
angle mapped in the legend. Well actually, for most purposes I am more
interested in the length but I guess there is no clever way for ggplot
to guess that from the data.

The most elegant solution would be what you propose first: add
aesthetics to geom_segment. But that would raise the problem of which
are required or not. Currently ggplot requires x, y and xend, yend.
With more arguments, it should require x, y and (xend, yend OR angle,
length) and I don't know whether that is doable.

Otherwise the new geom might be the way to go. In which case it might
even be nice to have two:
  - one with x,y, angle and length
  - one with x,y, u and v where u and v are the horizontal and
vertical component of a vector starting in x,y. This is a very common
representation for vector fields (think magnetic, electric, current,
wind etc.). All those things are far from statistics I agree, but R is
versatile enough to accommodate for them and there is interest in it
(I am in a marine physics and biology school and was asked to teach a
class on data manipulation and plotting in R, because they are trying
to get away from the omnipotent and pricy MATLAB).

Thanks in advance.

JiHO

messages.subject: Re: ordering of limits in scale_*_continuous
messages.body_plain:
library("ggplot2")

set.seed(1)
d=data.frame(a=runif(10),b=runif(10))

ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=b)) + scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,1))
# OK
ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=b)) + scale_y_continuous(limits=c(1,0))
# 10 rows removed

ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=-b)) +
scale_y_continuous(limits=c(-1,0))
# OK
ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=-b)) +
scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,-1))
# 10 rows removed

So indeed it looks like a bug. I initially thought it was only
occuring with a negative mapping of the data, as -b above. Basically
that it would cut out the data that was not on the plot based on the
original values rather than the transfromed(i.e. negative) ones. But
it seems more general than that.

JiHO

messages.subject: Setting/mapping x/y
messages.body_plain:
Some confusing things about mapping vs. setting:

df <- data.frame(a=1:10)

ggplot(data=df) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=a))

OK, this is exactly as expected.

ggplot(data=df) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=a,colour="blue"))

OK, this is exactly as expected.  The constant "blue" is being *mapped*, and displays as red.

ggplot(data=df) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=a,colour=13:14))  (or factor(13:14))

OK, this is mapping 13:14 to two colors, blue and red.

ggplot(data=df) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=a,colour=13))

Strange, this should be mapping the constant 13 to a constant color, I'd think, but in fact there is no plotting at all, and the scale is named "13" with a value of 14 represented as ... nothing.

ggplot(data=df) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=a,colour=13:14))

ggplot(data=df) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=a),colour="blue")

OK, exactly as expected.  The color is being set to blue.

ggplot(data=df) + geom_point(aes(x=a),y=23)

Strange, this gives an error (apply non-function).  Shouldn't this be 'setting' y to 23?

ggplot(data=df) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=23))

This works, though.

          -s

However, I am surprised that the scale key does not include the extreme value, namely 1 -- it shows 2,4,6,8,10. (True for scale_colour_gradient as well.)  I suppose it is looking for round numbers, and of course I can override this, and I'm not sure what I'd propose....

However:

ggplot(data=data.frame(a=1:10)) +
   geom_point(aes(x=a,y=a,colour=a)) +
   scale_colour_gradient2(low="red",high="blue",mid="green",midpoint=2)

has a surprising (to me) appearance.  Point (2,2) is indeed green, the stated midpoint, but point (1,1) is not red, but apparently 1/8 red + 7/8 green.  That is, it seems to be creating a balanced scale going from midpoint - max( max(r)-midpoint, midpoint-min(r) ) to midpoint + max( max(r)-midpoint, midpoint-min(r) ). Is that the intended behavior?

messages.subject: Re: Setting/mapping x/y
messages.body_plain:
Haldey will be the only one with a definitive answer to this but this
is my understanding:

On 2009-May-27  , at 12:23 , Stavros Macrakis wrote:

> ggplot(data=df) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=a,colour=13))
>
> Strange, this should be mapping the constant 13 to a constant color,
> I'd think, but in fact there is no plotting at all, and the scale is
> named "13" with a value of 14 represented as ... nothing.

My guess is that it interprets 13 as a color specification and 13 is
not a valid one so there is no color. How exactly the color is
interpreted depends on grid and the help of gpar reads:

      Colours can be specified in one of the forms returned by 'rgb', as
      a name (see 'colors') or as a positive integer index into the
      current palette (with zero or negative values being taken as
      transparent).

However
	ggplot(data=df) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=a,colour=1)
gives the same result even though:
	palette()
	[1] "black" "red" "green3" "blue" "cyan" "magenta" "yellow"
	[8] "gray"
i.e. palette()[1] exists.

So maybe ggplot is doing something with the color in between.

> ggplot(data=df) + geom_point(aes(x=a),y=23)
>
> Strange, this gives an error (apply non-function).  Shouldn't this
> be 'setting' y to 23?
>
> ggplot(data=df) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=23))
>
> This works, though.

This is probably because x and y and *required* aesthetics (as opposed
to colour etc. which can be only parameters). But I agree with you,
the first form should work and is more coherent with the concepts in
ggplot (well my understanding of them at least).
Actually, I think the second form even used to be invalid. At least
this construct:
	foo=23
	ggplot(data=df) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=foo))
used to be invalid for sure. To map something, you *had* to put in the
data frame specified by the data argument. This indeed made sense from
the grammar point of view (but the current behavior is often more
practical).

I hope that helps a bit.

JiHO

messages.subject: Re: scale_colour_gradient2
messages.body_plain:
On 2009-May-27  , at 13:06 , Stavros Macrakis wrote:

> This looks fine:
>
> ggplot(data=data.frame(a=1:10)) +
>    geom_point(aes(x=a,y=a,colour=a)) +
>
> scale_colour_gradient2(low="red",high="blue",mid="green",midpoint=5)
>
> 1 is mapped to red, 5 to blue, and 10 to green, which is good.
>
> However, I am surprised that the scale key does not include the
> extreme value, namely 1 -- it shows 2,4,6,8,10. (True for
> scale_colour_gradient as well.)  I suppose it is looking for round
> numbers, and of course I can override this, and I'm not sure what
> I'd propose....

I have also been bitten by that before: it is sometimes annoying that
the legend does not span the whole range of the data. However finding
the correct extremes is a tricky problem which might not have a
general solution (you would not want your legend to start at 0.587241
if that was your minimum). So the only sensible solution I can see
would be to force the min and max of the legend to match the min and
max of the data if those are integers (or close to integers). But that
would require writing something on top (or re-writing) pretty() which
is currently used to select the legends.

Plus, in the gradient2 case you have one additional constraint: you
probably also want to see your middle value. Therefore, in your case,
you would want:

	1 .. 2 .... 10

Unless you use two different intervals (i.e. call pretty 2 times) for
the part below 2 and above 2, I don't see an easy solution.

> However:
>
> ggplot(data=data.frame(a=1:10)) +
>    geom_point(aes(x=a,y=a,colour=a)) +
>
> scale_colour_gradient2(low="red",high="blue",mid="green",midpoint=2)
>
> has a surprising (to me) appearance.  Point (2,2) is indeed green,
> the stated midpoint, but point (1,1) is not red, but apparently 1/8
> red + 7/8 green.  That is, it seems to be creating a balanced scale
> going from midpoint - max( max(r)-midpoint, midpoint-min(r) ) to
> midpoint + max( max(r)-midpoint, midpoint-min(r) ). Is that the
> intended behavior?

I have no clue definitive answer once again. But I would guess it is
indeed intended because with a symmetric scale, the saturation of the
color is an indication of how far you are from the middle of the
scale. This information would be lost otherwise and could be
perceptually misleading (i.e. 1 and 10 would appear on-par in the plot).

JiHO

messages.subject_clean: Getting information about a ggplot object
messages.body_plain:
Hi Brandon,

This information doesn't exist until the plot is actually drawn - you
can change the data up until the last minute so it can't be
precomputed.  However, it's not hard to get the x ranges yourself:

rng <- c(
  round_any(min(test.data$values), binwidth, floor),
  round_any(max(test.data$values), binwidth, ceiling)
)

Alternatively, if you want both the x and y ranges, use the bin()
function which powers the histogram in ggplot2.

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: Quantile-quantile plot
messages.body_plain:
A followup to my earlier email....

On Thu, May 21, 2009 at 4:19 PM, Stavros Macrakis <macr...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I am trying to create a quantile-quantile plot of two sample distributions. ...
>
> However, I can't figure out how to do the usual beautiful ggplot slice-and-dice (colors, facets) with different subsets of the distributions....

What I ended up doing was building a data frame with the qq values precalculated.  This is not satisfactory in general because every possible combination of conditions that could be displayed needs to be precalculated.

What I am thinking of doing now is to put all the data in a single data frame and write a stat_ which takes an argument specifying the subsets to compare, something like this:

# Distributions to compare
dist1 <- data.frame( day = sample(7,200,replace=TRUE), traffic = c(rnorm(100,1,1),rnorm(100,3,1)) )
dist2 <- data.frame( day = sample(7,350,replace=TRUE), traffic = c(rnorm(50,2,1),rnorm(300,3,1)) )

df <- cbind( rbind(dist1,dist2), idx = c( rep(1:2, c(200,350) ) )

If I want to compare these distributions using a density plot, I can now do:

ggplot(data=df) +
  stat_density(aes(x=traffic,colour=idx),
               geom="path",
               position='identity') +        # btw, why do I get a warning if this is missing?
  facet_grid(. ~ day,margins=T)

One possible syntax for stat_qq (the current stat_qq should be renamed as stat_probability <http://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/probplot.htm> or something):

ggplot(data=df) +
  stat_qq(aes(x=traffic,y=traffic, axis=idx)) +
  facet_grid(. ~ day,margins=T)

but that has its own limitations.  For example, what if I want to compare N distributions against a reference distribution?  Or N against M?  Then again, that seems to be a more general problem -- which I'll write up as a separate email.

            -s

a white background; adjusting the opacity of the square is clearly
equivalent to simply changing the square to some degree of grey.

To simplify your search for what you want, I'd simply omit the fill
(which I believe is equivalent to setting fill='black') and play with
opacity until you get what you want.

messages.subject: Re: alpha and geom_rect
messages.body_plain:
Ah, my bad for not running your code. In your call to ggplot() you map
the colour aesthetic to a variable (which happens to have only 1
level), and that colour mapping is reused in geom_rect, hence the box
having a pink outline. To get rid of the outline, you should either
map color within the call to geom_point() only:

p = ggplot(data = testDF, aes(x1, y1))
p = p + geom_rect(aes(xmin = 3, xmax = 7, ymin = 3, ymax =7),alpha = 0.1)
p = p + geom_point(aes(colour='BAD'))

or set the color to "transparent" inside geom_rect():

p = ggplot(data = testDF, aes(x1, y1, colour = "BAD"))
p = p + geom_rect(aes(xmin = 3, xmax = 7, ymin = 3, ymax
=7),colour='transparent',alpha = 0.1)
p = p + geom_point()

Note that I've layered the points on top of the rect so that their
color isn't affected by the rect (which would diminish their luminance
and undermine your goal of calling attention to those points).

messages.subject: Re: alpha and geom_rect
messages.body_plain:
On 2009-May-29  , at 14:07 , Kasper Daniel Hansen wrote:

> I understand that there is some interaction between transparency and
> greyness. Let me restate my problem.
>
> geom_smooth produces exactly the effect I want. Using the default
> settings of geom_smooth in my call to geom_rect, I don't get the same
> grey/transparent scheme. I am baffled by this.

When I try this:

qplot(1:10, runif(10)*4) + geom_rect(aes(NULL, NULL, xmin = 3, xmax =
7, ymin = 3, ymax = 7), fill = "grey60", alpha = 0.4) + geom_smooth()

on a Quartz device, I get the exact same grey for the rectangle and
the smooth.
So it is something specific to how your example is written.

When I try that:

qplot(1:10, runif(10)*4) + geom_rect(aes(xmin = 3, xmax = 7, ymin = 3,
ymax = 7), fill = "grey60", alpha = 0.4) + geom_smooth()

the rectangle is opaque. What are the NULL, NULL for in your example?
Un-map x and y? But there are no x and y aes in geom_rect. There seem
to be an interaction between the definition of data in ggplot and the
fact that there is actually no data in geom_rect:

ggplot(data=data.frame(x=1:10, y=1:10)) + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y)) +
geom_rect(aes(xmin=3, xmax=6, ymin=3, ymax=6), alpha=0.5)
# opaque

ggplot() + geom_rect(aes(xmin=3, xmax=6, ymin=3, ymax=6), alpha=0.5)
# transparent

I would stick to a rule that works well for me: unless something is
common to *all* later geoms, do not supply it to ggplot(), only give
it to the appropriate geom. Here indeed:

ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y), data=data.frame(x=1:10, y=1:10))
+ geom_rect(aes(xmin=3, xmax=6, ymin=3, ymax=6), alpha=0.5)

works.

I hope that helps.

NB: an exception to the above rule is when faceting is involved: a
dataset containing all the facetting variables must be supplied to
ggplot.

JiHO
---

This one took me a while to figure out - the problem is that the
rectangle layer is inheriting the _data_, and even though you have not
mapped any variables to the data you still get one rectangle for each
row of the original dataset, i.e. ten rectangles plotted on top of one
another.

ggplot(data = testDF, aes(x1, y1, colour = "BAD")) + geom_point() +

    geom_rect(aes(xmin = 3, xmax = 7, ymin = 3, ymax =
7), fill = "grey60", alpha = 0.4, data = data.frame(x1 = 1, y1 = 1))

or

ggplot(data = testDF, aes(x1, y1, colour = "BAD")) + geom_point() +

   annotate("rect", xmin = 3, xmax = 7, ymin = 3, ymax = 7, fill =

"grey60", alpha = 0.4)

# but this is broken for this example in the current version, fixed in devel

Hadley

> row of the original dataset, i.e. ten rectangles plotted on top of one

Ah, I clearly didn't notice that.

Maybe this is a good example of why specifying data & mapping in
ggplot() can be dangerous. In teaching students ggplot2, I've come to
prefer telling them to explicitly specify their data & mapping within
each layer; indeed, I've been telling them to use
p=ggplot()
p=p+layer(
     geom=...
     ,geom_params=list(...)
     ,stat=...
     ,stat_params=list(...)
     ,data=...
     ,mapping=...
     ,position=...
)
just to be extra explicit. I find it also reinforces the grammar.

Mike

p <-
ggplot(dat) +
geom_line( aes_string(x="Timep", y=y, group="PID"))+

scale_x_continuous(name=xlab) +

}

messages.subject: Changing aesthetic mappings.
messages.body_plain:
On p. 47 of the current ggplot draft, examples are provided regarding
changing aesthetic mappings.  The following sequence of R code is provided:

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg, y = wt))
p + geom_point()
p + geom_point(aes(colour = factor(cyl)))
p + geom_point(aes(y = disp))

I don't understand the plot generated by the last of these statements
(displayed on the right side on p. 48).

1.  The marginal of the scatterplot indicates that y has been correctly
remapped to disp, so why is the y axis still labeled wt?
2.  The colour mapping for factor(cyl) was not explicitly overridden, so why
isn't this mapping still in effect in the plot?

messages.subject: Re: Changing aesthetic mappings.
messages.body_plain:
hello,

On Sun, May 31, 2009 at 08:43:46AM -0400, Jim Watkins wrote:
>
> On p. 47 of the current ggplot draft, examples are provided regarding
> changing aesthetic mappings.  The following sequence of R code is provided:
>
> p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg, y = wt))
> p + geom_point()
> p + geom_point(aes(colour = factor(cyl)))
> p + geom_point(aes(y = disp))
>
> I don't understand the plot generated by the last of these statements
> (displayed on the right side on p. 48).
>
> 1.  The marginal of the scatterplot indicates that y has been correctly
> remapped to disp, so why is the y axis still labeled wt?

It's written on the same page:

| Aesthetic mappings specified in a layer
| act _nly that layer. For that reason, unless you modify the default
| scales, axis labels and legend titles will be based on the plot defaults.

and the default was set with ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg, y = wt)).

> 2.  The colour mapping for factor(cyl) was not explicitly overridden, so why
> isn't this mapping still in effect in the plot?

because the mapping is not written to p. What you are thinking of is:

p <- p + geom_point(aes(colour = factor(cyl)))

p + geom_point(aes(y = disp))

regards,
 stefan
